blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

The thing that started this book was a number. Between 1920 and 1930, two hundred and eight people came to the United States from Persia. Not two hundred thousand. Two hundred and eight, in ten years.

Think about what that means for one of them. No neighborhood. No restaurant that makes the food you grew up on. Nobody in the state who can say your name, and no one to talk to in your own language, possibly ever again.

Then the Depression comes, a quarter of the country is out of work, and people start counting who belongs. Nobody had to pass a law. When there are ten men for one job, the foreign one goes last. So he takes work nobody else wants — which is how a man ends up shuffling in circles for forty-six days in front of a paying crowd, while an announcer calls him a name that isn’t his because the real one is too much bother.

I gave him the only thing he could carry across an ocean for free, which is a story. The Shahnameh is a thousand years old, and it is full of people who don’t recognize each other until it’s too late. A father fights a stranger, kills him, and finds out afterward it was his son. I’ve never known whether that’s about fate or about something smaller — how easy it is not to say who you are, and how long you can go on not saying it.

I didn’t have to make the dance marathons worse than they were. People really danced for six weeks, sleeping fifteen minutes an hour while still moving, held up by a partner. Men died on the floor and the band kept playing. It worked because a country that couldn’t stand to look at its own suffering could pay a quarter to watch somebody else’s.
Chew Z
I. FORTY-FIVE AND FIFTEEN
1. THE PHYSICAL
The sign had been up on Jefferson Avenue for eleven days and Alma had walked past it nine times before she went in.

It was painted on a bedsheet and hung off the front of a building that used to sell Studebakers. The showroom windows were soaped over. Somebody had done the lettering in red and then gone back over it in gold, which meant somebody had cared, and the gold had run in the second line so it looked like the words were bleeding upward.
MARATHON DANCE $1,000 IN CASH THEY GO TILL THEY DROP
Underneath, smaller, in a hand that had gotten tired: Doyle Ferrin Presents.
She went in at four in the afternoon on a Saturday with sixty cents in her coat and the coat buttoned to the throat because the dress under it had been washed too many times to be seen in daylight.

The showroom had been cleared. They’d taken the cars out and taken the counters out and laid a floor down over the concrete, real maple, and the smell of the varnish was still in the air and made her think, stupidly, of a school. Around three sides they’d built up plank bleachers. Along the fourth was a low stage with a piano on it and a drum kit and six chairs, and above the stage a board the size of a door, blank, with a row of little brass hooks screwed into it.
There was a line of maybe forty people at a card table.
“Name.”

The man at the table did not look up. He had a ledger and a fountain pen and a cigarette going in a coffee saucer and he was working fast, the way a man works when he’s been told what he’ll be paid regardless.
“Alma Sutter.”
“Age.”
“Twenty-nine.”
“Partner.”
“I don’t have one.”
Now he looked up. He had a long face and a small mouth and he was somewhere past forty and his shirt was clean, which in that room was a kind of shouting.
“You come alone.”
“Yes.”
“Married?”
She said, “My husband’s in Toledo,” which was true, and let him do the rest of it himself, which he did.

He wrote something. “We got four girls without partners and eleven fellas. You’ll get matched. You don’t get to pick and you don’t get to trade. Once you’re paired you’re paired till one of you goes down.” He turned the ledger around and put the pen on it. “Read that and sign it.”
She read the first two lines and then read the rest of it the way you read a thing you have already decided to sign.

The undersigned enters of her own free will and holds harmless Ferrin Amusement Co. of Toledo, Ohio, its agents and employees, against injury, illness, collapse, permanent disability, or death arising from participation.
The undersigned agrees that the decision of the judges is final in all matters.
The undersigned agrees to abide by all rules as posted and as amended at any time and without notice.
The undersigned certifies that all statements given upon entry are true.
She held the pen a second on that last one.
“Dependents,” the man said. He’d gone back to writing. “Anybody at home. We put it in the program.”
The room went on around her. Somebody on the bleachers laughed at something. A boy was up on a ladder screwing the last of the brass hooks into the board.
“I had a little girl,” Alma said.
The pen stopped.
“Had.”
“July.”
He looked at her then for what felt like a long while and was probably two seconds, and something moved behind the small mouth that she would think about many times later and never be able to name.

“I’m sorry to hear it,” he said, and he was — that was the thing, he really was, she’d have sworn to it — and then he wrote it down, and while he was writing he said, in exactly the same voice, “How old.”
“Four.”
“Name?”
“Ruth.”
He wrote that too. Then he blotted it and turned the ledger back around and said, “Doyle Ferrin,” and put his hand out, and she shook it, and his hand was dry and warm.
“Doc’s in back,” he said. “Through there. Then you’re in.”

The doctor was a young man with a bad shave who had set up in what used to be the parts department. He listened to her chest with a stethoscope he had to warm in his palm first, and looked in her ears, and asked her to walk to the wall and back, and watched her feet the whole way with more attention than any man had given her in a year.
“Take the shoes off.”
She took them off.
He turned her left foot over in his hands like something at a market. “You been on your feet.”
“I was at the laundry on Vernor till May.”
“Standing?”
“Standing.”
He put the foot down. “You got a high arch. That’s good for about three hundred hours. After that it isn’t.” He wrote on his card. “You understand the arch is going to come down.”
“Come down.”

“Flatten. Permanently. Most of the girls that go long, it happens.” He said it the way you’d say it looks like rain. “Once it comes down it doesn’t go back up. You’ll walk different the rest of your life.”
Alma looked at her own feet on the cold floor of a parts department, and thought about the rest of her life, and found that it had gotten very short and very simple and had one thing in it.
“How long is three hundred hours,” she said.
“Twelve, thirteen days.”
“And the contest runs?”
The doctor laughed once, without any humor in it at all, and wrote something else on the card.
“Lady,” he said, “the last one of these I worked ran forty-one days.”

They put her in a green dress from a rack of them. Doyle had bought a lot of forty from a dressmaker in Toledo that went under in the spring, and they were all the same green, and they would be in every photograph anybody ever took of her.
A woman in white pinned the number 63 to her back. She was fifty-some with hands like a bricklayer’s and a voice like she’d already told you twice.
“I’m Ida,” she said. “I’m the nurse. You’ll see more of me than you’ll see of God.” She worked the second pin through. “You got anything in you now? Anything you take?”
“No.”
“You will.” Ida turned her around by the shoulders and looked at her, not unkindly, and put a thumb under her jaw and turned her head to the light. “Twenty-nine?”
“Yes.”

“Eat everything they put in front of you. Every time. Even when you can’t. Especially when you can’t.” She let go. “And keep your mouth shut about your feet. You go to the doc, he tells Doyle, and Doyle finds a way to make it a thing.”
“A thing.”
“A story, hon,” Ida said. “Everything in here is a story. They pay a quarter for it.”
At half past eight they let the crowd in.

Alma stood at the edge of the maple with the other unmatched women and watched the bleachers fill and could not get her mind around it. It was a Saturday night in the third year of the worst thing that had ever happened to any of them and there were, she would read later in the Free Press, nineteen hundred people in that room. They had all found a quarter. They had all decided that this was what the quarter was for.
A boy of about fifteen went up a ladder at the back of the stage and hung a single brass numeral on the first hook of the board.
The band came out. Six of them, and the piano player was a big soft man in a jacket the color of a plum who sat down without looking at anybody and cracked his knuckles one hand at a time.
Then Doyle Ferrin came out with a microphone on a cord and the room stood up.

He was good. She hadn’t expected him to be good. He got them laughing in under a minute and he did it without saying anything funny, just by the rhythm of it, the way he’d lay something down and wait and then pick it up again, and Alma understood that whatever else this was, it was the man’s trade, and he was better at his trade than she had ever been at hers.

“Ninety-one couples,” Doyle said. “Forty-five minutes on. Fifteen minutes off. Around the clock. Cots come out at midnight and you can watch ’em sleep, folks, that’s included in the price of admission and there’s no other show in Michigan where you can say that.”
Laughter.
“Rule number one. You keep moving. Rule number two.” He let it sit. “If one goes down — both go home.”
And the room made a sound Alma had never heard before, a low warm ohhh, nineteen hundred people receiving good news.
They called the unmatched to the middle of the floor.

Four women in green and eleven men in shirtsleeves, standing in the light in front of everybody, while Doyle worked the crowd about it — look at this, folks, look what we got left over — and Alma kept her eyes on the maple and thought about a boy in a photograph she did not have, and about the fact that she had never in her life been looked at by more than about thirty people at once.
“Number sixty-three,” Doyle said. “Mrs. Sutter, come out here.”
She came out.

“And let’s see.” He walked the line of men. He was enjoying it. He put his hand on one and moved on, and on the third he stopped and turned around and grinned at the bleachers with the whole of his face.
“Well now,” he said. “Folks, we got ourselves a prince.”
The man he’d stopped at was maybe thirty. Black hair, a good jaw gone thin, sleeves rolled twice, and he had the stillness of somebody standing in a room he has decided not to be surprised by.
“What’s the name, friend?”
The man said it.
Doyle put the microphone closer. “Say again?”
He said it again.
“Bah— ” Doyle looked at the crowd and the crowd laughed, and he laughed with them, and it was the friendliest sound in the world. “Folks, I can’t get around that one. Where’s that from, friend?”
“Persia.”

“Persia.” Doyle said it the way you’d unwrap something. “Ladies and gentlemen, all the way from Persia. That’s your Arabian Nights, that’s your flying carpets. That’s your sheiks.” He put a hand up against the noise. “Now what do we call you, pal, on account of I got to say it four hundred times.”
The man looked at Doyle for a moment.
“Bahram,” he said.
“Barney,” Doyle said.
The bleachers went up like a struck match.

Alma watched the man’s face while it happened. There was nothing on it. He waited out the noise, and then he put his hand out toward her, palm up, the way you would offer to help somebody down off a step, and he said, under all of it, so quietly that only she could possibly have heard:
“Not one word from that man is going to be true. It will be easier if you know it now.”
She put her hand in his.
At nine o’clock the boy took the numeral off the hook and hung up a 1, and the band started, and ninety-one couples began to move.
2. COT CALL
The first thing she learned was that nobody danced.

She had come in braced for dancing. She had thought about it on the walk over — that she would have to hold a stranger and move to music in front of a crowd, and that this would be the humiliating part — and inside of forty minutes she understood that dancing was not what this was, that dancing was a word Doyle Ferrin used on a bedsheet to get people through a door.
What it was, was walking. Two people holding each other loosely and walking in a slow counterclockwise circle on a maple floor while a band played, and never stopping.
“Don’t lift your feet,” the man said.
“What?”

“You are lifting your feet.” He had a low voice and a careful way of putting a sentence down, like a man setting a full cup on a table. “Slide them. Do not lift them. You will lift them nine thousand times tonight and by tomorrow you will not be able to.”
She tried it. It felt ridiculous, a shuffle, an old woman’s walk.
“Better.”
“How do you know that?”
“I don’t. A man told me at the door.” He turned them a little to take the corner. “He was very sure.”
At forty-five minutes the air horn went off.

It was mounted over the stage and it was the loudest thing Alma had ever been in a room with. Ninety-one couples came off the floor in a body, through a gap in the bleachers, into the old parts department where they had set up the cots in two long rows, women’s side and men’s side, with a canvas hung between.
Fifteen minutes.

She lay down in the green dress with her shoes on because a woman on the next cot told her not to take them off — you take ’em off tonight and tomorrow they won’t go back on — and she looked at the ceiling and did not sleep at all, and it seemed to her that she had barely got flat before the horn went again.
That was hour one.
The eighth hour was when she understood the shape of the thing.

Not the pain. There wasn’t any pain yet, that was the trick of it, that was why ninety-one couples had signed. It was that the fifteen minutes had stopped being a rest and become a thing that was taken away from her. She would lie down and count the ceiling boards and the horn would go, and it was as though somebody was standing over her stealing it out of her hands, every hour, forever.
“You are counting,” the man said.
“I’m not doing anything.”
“You are counting the minutes off. I can feel it in your arm.” He steered them past the bandstand. “Don’t. Not tonight. Tonight is easy and you are spending yourself on it.”
“You’ve done this.”
“No.”
“Then how — ”
“Because I have done other things.” He said it without any weight and she let it go.
At midnight they brought the cots out onto the floor.

Alma had heard Doyle say it and had not really taken it in, and now here it was: eight iron cots wheeled out under the lights on the maple in front of the bleachers, and Doyle at the microphone explaining, warmly, that folks, these here are your leaders, these are the eight couples the judges like best tonight, and they’re going to take their rest right here where you can see ’em.

She and the Persian were not among the eight. That was luck. She watched a girl of maybe twenty from Wyandotte lie down on a cot in the middle of a maple floor and put her forearm over her eyes and go to sleep, actually go to sleep, with nineteen hundred people looking at her and a spotlight on her face, and Alma felt something turn over in her stomach that had nothing to do with tiredness.
“They are the lucky ones,” the man said.
“How is that lucky.”

“Because they will not have to walk while they sleep.” He was quiet a moment. “In two weeks you will want that cot very badly. You will want them to put you in the light so you can lie down. You should know that about yourself early. It will save you from being surprised.”
He corrected Doyle twice.

The first time was on the second night, at the eleven o’clock, when Doyle came around the floor with the microphone doing what he did — leaning in on a couple, getting a name, getting a story, moving on — and got to them and said, “And here’s Barney the Persian Prince, folks, and his lovely partner Alma. Barney, tell the folks about the harem.”
The band did a little sting on the cymbal.
And the man said, pleasantly, into the microphone, “There is no harem. I worked eleven years at the Rouge.”
It got a laugh. It got a good laugh, actually, and Alma felt him relax half an inch, and Doyle laughed too and said something and moved on.
The second time was four nights later.

Doyle had settled into calling him the Sheik. It had come up out of the crowd, somebody in the bleachers had shouted it, and Doyle had taken it the way he took everything, gratefully, and made it his own inside of an evening. There he goes, folks, the Sheik of Ecorse.

And on the fifth night Bahram stopped, mid-circle, which you were allowed to do so long as you kept your feet going, and he said to Doyle, not into the microphone this time, without heat, the way you would tell a man his shoelace was undone:
“A sheik is an Arab. I am not an Arab. Persia is a different country and a different language and the difference is about as large as the difference between you and a Frenchman.”
Doyle looked at him with real interest.
“That so,” he said.
“That is so.”
“Huh,” Doyle said, and nodded slowly, and turned away with the microphone still live and said, “Ladies and gentlemen — the Sheik of Ecorse!”
And nineteen hundred people cheered.
Alma waited until they had gone around twice.
“You could say it again,” she said.
“No.”
“He might — ”

“He knows.” The man was looking straight ahead over her shoulder at the far bleachers. “He knew before I said it the first time. He has a map behind that stage with pins in it, he has been in ninety towns, he knows where Persia is. That is what I did not understand until just now.” He took the corner. “He is not making a mistake. There is no mistake to correct.”
He said it flatly and without any self-pity at all, and then he said:
“So. Barney.”
“I won’t call you that.”
“You will,” he said. “Everyone will. It is shorter.” And after a moment, in a slightly different voice: “It is a small thing. I have had smaller things cost me more.”

That was the second correction and there was never a third. Alma kept count of that without meaning to, the way you keep count of a dripping tap, and eleven hundred hours later, when she was seventy-one years old and the whole thing had gone as far into the past as her own childhood, the two corrections were still there, sitting in her like two stones in a coat pocket, and she still could not have said why they were the part she couldn’t put down.
He answered to Barney by the second week.
By the third week the newspapers had it.

By the fifth week there were nineteen hundred people in Wayne County who believed, without ever having thought about it for one second, that they had personally met a man named Barney from Arabia, and there was exactly one person in the building who knew what he was actually called, and she was too tired to say it out loud.
3. FORTY-FIVE AND FIFTEEN
Thirty-one couples went in the first two days.

Alma had not expected that either. She had thought it would be a slow thinning, one here and one there, and instead it was a slaughter — boys who’d come in on a dare, a pair of sisters who lasted nine hours, a man of fifty who sat down on the floor at four in the morning of the second day and simply would not get up again, not for the judge, not for his partner, not for anybody, and had to be walked out with his arm over a man’s shoulder while the crowd applauded him and Doyle said something kind.

The kind things were the worst. She noticed that early. Doyle never mocked anybody on the way out. He gave them a send-off, he got the crowd to give them a hand, he said let’s hear it for a fella that gave us everything he had — and it was so generous, and it made you want so badly to be the one still standing when it was said about somebody else, that Alma understood by the third morning that the kindness was part of the machinery and possibly the most expensive part.
By Tuesday there were sixty couples. By Thursday, fifty-one.
The days had no shape. That was the thing nobody told you.

Forty-five minutes on and fifteen off, and the fifteen went by like a hand passing over a candle, and so the whole of your life became one continuous hour that kept starting over. There was no morning. There was no evening. There was a moment when the crowd got bigger and a moment when it got smaller, and the crowd was the only clock.

They ate twelve times a day. Standing up, moving, plates held at the chest. Eggs at some hours, and a stew at some hours, and always coffee, and always bread, and the food was actually not bad — Doyle Ferrin fed them properly and made sure the Free Press knew he fed them properly — and it was the same eleven or twelve things in rotation forever.
“What is this,” Bahram said on the fourth day, looking into the bowl.
“Beef stew.”
“It is not.”
“It’s beef stew, Barney.”
“It is water that has met beef.” He ate it anyway, all of it, quickly. He always ate all of it. “I want you to understand that I am not complaining. I am reporting.”
They set their arrangement in the first week without ever discussing it, the way people do.
He took the outside of the circle, which was longer, and she took the inside, which was shorter, and he did that without saying so and denied it when she said so.

He talked and she didn’t. He had worked out by the third day that she would go somewhere behind her own eyes if the silence got long enough, and that she came back slower each time, and so he talked — about nothing, about the band, about a foreman he’d had at the Rouge who used to weigh his own lunch on a scale — and she made a sound now and then to show she was there.
And they worked out the sleeping.

That was the strange one. Around the sixtieth hour you stopped being able to keep your eyes open on the floor, and the answer, which every single person in that building arrived at independently and none of them were taught, was that you slept standing up while your partner walked you.

You put your head on their shoulder and you went out. Ten seconds, thirty seconds, sometimes two or three minutes. Your legs kept going. That was the part Alma never got used to and never stopped thinking about afterward: that her legs kept going. She would come up out of it in a different corner of the room, with the music at a different place in the song, and her feet would have covered forty feet of maple without her.

The judges allowed it. There was a rule that your knees couldn’t touch the floor and that was the whole of it. A judge would come along and put two fingers under your chin and lift, to see whether the eyes came open, and if they came open at all you were fine.
“Your turn,” he’d say, and she’d put her head down on the wool of his shoulder.
Then, later, “My turn,” and he’d put his down on her, and she’d take his weight, and he was heavier than he looked and got lighter every week.
Ida came around every four hours with the bottle.
It was brown glass with no label and she poured it into a little tin cup and there was a second bottle, a smaller one, that came out only at night.
“What is it,” Alma asked the first time.
“That one’ll keep you up.” Ida held out the cup. “The other one’ll put you down. You want the down one at cot call, not now.”
“But what is it?”
“Hon,” Ida said, “it’s four dollars a week and I don’t ask.”

It tasted like licorice and something underneath the licorice that was not licorice. It went down warm. Twenty minutes later Alma noticed that the cymbals had gotten louder, which she assumed meant the drummer had gotten louder, and it was three weeks before she understood that the drummer had had nothing to do with it.
Bahram took his and did not comment.
“You’ve had that before,” she said.
“Something like it.”
“Where?”

He was quiet for a bit. Then: “There is a foundry job at the Rouge where you stand in front of an open door. The men who did that job were given something in their coffee in the summer of 1929, from a nurse, in a cup, and nobody asked what it was, and it tasted of licorice.” He shrugged with the shoulder she wasn’t using. “It is the same country. It is only a different room.”
The first hard night was hour seventy-something.

She stopped being able to feel her right foot from the arch forward. Not numb exactly — it had gone strange, it had become an object she was operating, a thing at the end of her leg that reported back late.
She started to go down at the far corner by the fire door, and she knew she was going, and there was a long strange moment in which she watched herself go and had no opinion about it at all.
He caught her under both arms and got a knee behind her knee and walked her, and it took maybe eight seconds, and no judge saw it.
When she came back up he was talking. He had not stopped talking.
“ — and the pier at Bandar, which is not a pier, it is four boards, and I stood on it with a bag and I was twenty-two years old and I had never in my life been out of sight of the mountain — ”
“Barney.”
“ — so you can imagine — ”
“Barney. I’m here.”
“I know,” he said. “I was talking so that you would have somewhere to come back to.”

The band went into something slow. Fitz had a way of doing that when the floor started to look bad, dropping the tempo without being asked, and Doyle let him, because Doyle knew the difference between the show he was selling tonight and the show he was selling in five weeks.
Alma got her foot back around hour seventy-eight.
“Thank you,” she said.
“It is not a favor,” Bahram said. “If you go down, I go with you. You understand that this is the only reason anyone in this room is kind to anyone.”
“Is that true?”

He thought about it honestly. She would learn that he always thought about things honestly, that he was incapable of the small automatic lie that oiled every other conversation she’d ever had, and that this was going to be either the best or the worst thing about him.
“No,” he said at last. “But it is true enough to say out loud.”
4. AFTER YOU
They lost ninety seconds a night to good manners and it took her nine days to find out why.

It happened at the horn. The horn would go and the couples would come off the maple and there was a bottleneck at the gap in the bleachers, one door’s width for a hundred people, and everybody in that building shoved except the two of them.
The first night she’d thought it was chivalry. He stood back at the gap and put a hand out — please — and she went through, and that was that, and it cost them maybe four seconds.

By the second week the bottleneck had gotten worse, because the couples that were left were slower, and the four seconds had become fifteen, and Alma had started saying no, you go, your feet are worse than mine, and he had started saying my feet are excellent, please, and they would stand in the gap while forty people went around them, having a small polite argument, losing rest they could not get back.
“This is insane,” she said, on the ninth day, lying down with eleven minutes left of fifteen.
“Yes.”
“Then go first.”
“After you.”
“Barney.”
“That is not something I can do,” he said, from the men’s side of the canvas, in the dark. “I am aware of how it sounds.”
“Why not?”
There was a long pause and she thought he’d gone to sleep, which was the correct use of the time.

“There is a thing we do,” he said. “It does not have a word in English. You offer, and the other person refuses, and you offer again, and they refuse again, and you offer a third time, and then they accept. Three times. If they accept the first time, they are a peasant. If you only offer once, you are a liar.” She heard him turn over. “You cannot buy a melon in Tabriz in under four minutes.”
“That’s the stupidest thing I ever heard.”
“It is.”
“Then why do you do it?”
“Because I am thirty years old,” he said, “and it is in my hands.”
She started timing it after that, for something to do.
Hour 214: eleven seconds. Hour 215: nine. Hour 216: twenty-two, because Ida had got in behind them and joined in, saying oh, go on, go on, and made it a three-body problem.
“You know what this is costing us,” Alma said.
“Ninety seconds a night.”
“You knew?”

“I have known since the fourth night. I have been doing the arithmetic for a week.” He steered her past the stage. “Ninety seconds a night, forty-six nights. It is one hour and nine minutes of sleep.”
“You could just walk through the door.”
“Yes.”
“Then — ”
“You could accept the first offer,” he said.
She opened her mouth and shut it again.
“There it is,” he said. “You cannot either. Because in your country if a woman goes through a door in front of a man who has held it, she is — what is the word. Fast.”
“That’s not — ” She stopped. “That’s not the same.”

“No. It is exactly the same and it is a different word.” He was smiling; she could hear it without looking. “The difference is that yours is invisible to you. Mine is a costume. Everyone can see mine.”
The cultural instruction went both ways and neither of them was any good at it.
He could not understand how are you. He had been in the country eight years and it still stopped him.
“A man at the meal counter asked me how I was.”
“He was being friendly.”

“I told him.” Bahram sounded genuinely aggrieved. “I told him that my back was bad and that I had not seen my mother’s grave and that I did not think I would win this contest. And he looked at me as if I had put my hand in his pocket.”
“You’re supposed to say fine.”
“Even if I am not fine.”
“Especially if you’re not fine.”
“So it is not a question.”
“It’s not a question.”
“Then why,” he said, with real feeling, “is it shaped like one.”

She, for her part, spent most of the first two weeks under the impression that Persia was somewhere near Egypt, that he had grown up around camels, and that Persian was a kind of cat and also a kind of rug and had nothing to do with a country.
“There is a rug,” he conceded. “There are many rugs. My uncle sold rugs. I am not going to pretend the rugs are a slander.”
“And the cat?”
“The cat is a Turkish cat,” he said, “and it is a long story and it makes me angry.”

She laughed. It surprised them both. It was hour two hundred and something and it was the first time she had laughed since June, and the sound came out of her wrong, cracked in the middle, and she put her face down on his shoulder so nobody in the bleachers would see it happen.
He walked her in a slow circle and did not say anything about it.

That was the other thing about him, and it took her longer to notice than the manners: he let things be. Every other person she had met since July had wanted her to do something with her face. Look up, chin up, there’s a girl, smile now. He just walked.

There was one more piece of the arrangement and it got settled that same week, at the gap in the bleachers, at hour two hundred and thirty, when a boy from Wyandotte tried to push past them and Bahram put a forearm out and stopped him without appearing to move at all.
“After you,” Bahram said to Alma.
“After you.”
“After you.”
“After you.”

And Ida, coming up behind with the bottles, said, “Oh for the love of Christ,” and put a hand flat on each of their backs and shoved them both through the door at once, sideways, jammed in the frame together, and the whole women’s side of the parts department laughed at them, and it was the best thing that happened in the first thousand hours.
After that, they went through together. It cost four seconds.
They still did the argument. They just did it moving.
5. THE FIRST ONE DOWN
The song came out of nothing on a Wednesday.

Doyle had written it himself. He admitted that freely, at the microphone, the way he admitted everything — folks, I wrote this on a train outside Sandusky and I want you to know it took me nine minutes — and Fitz had put a tune under it, a slow one in a walking tempo, and the deal was that the band played it every time a couple went out.
It went:
The bank took the farm and the farm took the man,
I got two left shoes and a coffee can,
But the sign said DANCE and I said I can —
So hold me up till the horn.

The first time she heard it, a boy and a girl from Lincoln Park were being walked off with their arms around a judge, and the crowd was singing along by the second line, because Doyle had taught it to them the night before on purpose.
By the fourth week Alma could not get it out of her head at any hour of the day. It got in under everything. It was in her feet.
They lost couple number thirty-one on the same night and Doyle added a verse.

That was the arrangement, and he announced it as though it were a tribute. Every couple that goes out, folks, they get a verse. That’s their verse. It belongs to them now. And the couple going out would be crying with exhaustion and gratitude at the door, and the band would play the new verse, and nineteen hundred people would learn it, and it would be theirs forever.
Fifteen minutes is a mighty short night,
Forty-five is a mighty long fight,
And the fella keeps score by the ceiling light —
So hold me up till the horn.
“He is very good at this,” Bahram said.
“He’s terrible.”
“He is both.” He turned them at the corner. “Do you know what the song does?”
“It’s a song.”
“It teaches them that going out is beautiful,” he said. “It is the most useful thing in this building. In two weeks, when you are finished, you will not want to stop. You will want your verse.”
She stopped talking on the eighty-eighth hour and did not start again for most of a day.
There was no reason. Nothing had happened. She had gotten through the door for the fifteen and lain down on the cot and looked at the ceiling and something in her had simply put its tools down.
She got up at the horn and walked and did not answer him.

He tried three things. He tried a question, and she didn’t answer it. He tried a joke about the stew. He tried silence, and after about half an hour of silence he did something she felt in her spine: he took his hand off her back for a second and put it down again lower and tighter, the way you’d take hold of something on a slope.

“I am going to talk now,” he said, “and you do not have to say anything at all. But I want you to listen, because if you go where you are going I will not be able to reach you and then we will both be walking out that door tonight.”
She said nothing.
“There was a man,” he said, “and he was the first man.”
The band was playing something with brushes on the snare.

“He lived in the mountains and he wore the skins of animals because nobody had made cloth yet. Nobody had made anything yet. He was the first, so everything that existed, he was the one who had to think of it. Fire. Cooking a thing before you eat it. He had a son, and he loved his son the way you love a thing when there is only one of it in the world, and something came out of the dark and killed the boy.”
Alma kept walking.

“And that is the first story,” Bahram said. “Not the making of the world. The world was already there. The first story is a father who has to go on being the first man after his son is dead, because there is nobody else to be it.”
They went around the corner by the fire door.
“What happened to him,” she said.
It came out of her like a splinter coming out.
“He wept for a year,” Bahram said, “and then he went to war, and he won, and it did not help. It is very old. Nobody had thought yet to say that it helped.”

She asked him where it came from and he said it was from a book, and she said what book, and he said the book, and she said what, and he looked at her with an expression she would learn to recognize as a man deciding whether to be insulted.

“It is a poem,” he said. “It is called the Shahnameh. That means the Book of Kings, and that is exactly what is in it — kings, in order, from the first one to the last.” He turned them at the corner. “It is sixty thousand lines. Everyone where I am from knows some of it and nobody has read all of it. It took one man thirty years to write.”
“Like the Arabian Nights.”
There was a pause of a length that she felt in her teeth.
“No,” Bahram said.
“Well, it — ”

“No. The Arabian Nights is a woman telling a king stories so that he will not cut her head off in the morning. It is a wonderful book. It is Arab and Indian and Persian and it is about stories.” He was walking faster; she had to adjust. “This is not that. This is what happened. Or — ” and he pulled himself back, visibly, “— it is what we say happened. Kings and years and the names of their sons. It is the history of the world up until the part where the history gets written down by clerks and becomes boring.”
“You’re angry.”
“I am not angry.”
“Barney.”
“I am a little angry,” he said, “and I would like to state that it is not with you, it is with a man in Ohio in 1926 who told me that where I come from is a place where people ride carpets.”
They went out onto the floor at the horn and Doyle was already going, working the crowd for the eleven o’clock, and the band came in behind him.
They give you a cot and they give you a spot,
They give you a number, they give you a lot,
They give you everything, mister, but what you ain’t got —
So hold me up till the horn.
Somewhere behind the bleachers a couple was crying and being congratulated.
“Tell me the next one,” Alma said.
“Not tonight.”
“Why not.”
“Because you have started listening,” Bahram said, “and that is worth more than a story. I am going to make it last.”
6. TABRIZ
There were forty-four couples left when the Free Press sent a man out.

He came on a Sunday afternoon with a photographer and stayed two hours, and Doyle walked him around the floor like a tenant showing an apartment. The photograph they ran on the Monday was of the Wyandotte girl asleep on a cot under a spotlight, and it was a good photograph, and it sold a great many quarter admissions, and the caption did not have her name in it.
The story called Bahram a Persian, known to the crowd as Barney.
He read it twice and folded it and gave it back to her and said nothing about it at all, which was how she learned to tell when something had gone into him.
He told her about the mountain that night, in the small hours, when the bleachers were down to about sixty people and the band was three men.

“Tabriz is in the north,” he said. “It is high. There is a mountain called Sahand and it is on your left when you go out of the city to the south and it is the first thing I ever saw and the last thing. Everything in my life until I was twenty-two happened where I could see that mountain.”
“What was your house like?”
“Small. Flat roof. In the summer we slept on the roof.” He walked her past the stage. “You cannot imagine it and I am not going to try to make you. It was a house.”
“Did you have brothers?”
“No.”
“Sisters?”
“No.” He took a breath. “There was one of me, and there was my mother, and there was a very great deal of quiet.”
She waited.
“My father left in the winter of 1911,” he said. “I was nine.”
He told it plainly, in the order it happened, without decorating it, and she understood by the fourth sentence that he had told it before and probably to himself.

There had been Americans in Persia. That was the part she couldn’t get her mind around. In 1911 the government in Tehran had been broke and badly governed and half-eaten by the Russians and the British, and somebody had had the idea of hiring an American to come and run the treasury — an actual American, from Washington — and he had come, with a staff, and Bahram’s father had been one of the Persian men who worked for them.
“He was a clerk. He wrote numbers in a book. He was very proud of it, that he worked for the Americans, and I remember that he began to wear a different collar.”
“What happened?”

“The Russians did not like it. They put soldiers on the road to Tehran and they gave the government two days to send the Americans home, and the government sent them home.” He was quiet a moment. “That is the whole of it. Two days. A country decides something in two days and forty years happen to you because of it.”
“And your father went with them.”

“My father went with them.” He turned them at the corner. “He said he would send for us. He said six months. He was not lying — I want to be accurate about this, because it took me twenty years to be accurate about it. He was not lying when he said it. He meant it in the room, out loud, with his hand on my head.”
The band went into the song for a couple going out, somewhere behind them, and the crowd sang.

“He wrote for two years,” Bahram said. “Then he wrote less. Then there was a war and everybody stopped writing. My mother kept the letters in a tin that had been a tin of English biscuits and she read them in an order that she had worked out and she never told me what the order was.”
“When did she die?”
“1919. There was famine in the north. It was not one thing that killed her, it was the whole of that year.” He said it evenly. “I was seventeen. I sold the house and I kept the tin.”
“So you came here to find him.”
“No,” Bahram said, too fast, and then, “yes. Of course. Yes.”
They went around.

“I told myself it was work,” he said. “I told the man at the consulate it was work. I told myself for four years on the way — because it took four years, I did not get on a ship and arrive, I went to Baku and I went to Constantinople and I was in Constantinople for nineteen months painting numbers on buses — and every single day of it I told myself I was going to America because America is where the work is.”
“And?”
“And that was also true,” he said. “That is the thing that nobody explains to you about a lie you tell yourself. It is not that it is false. It is that it is true and it is not the reason.”
Alma put her head down on his shoulder for a while.
When she came up he was still walking, and the room had gone that particular green-brown color it went at four in the morning, and he said, as though there had been no gap:
“I chose my name on the boat.”
“You what?”

“My mother called me Abbas. It is a fine name. Half the men in the city are called it.” He shrugged. “On the boat there was a man from Rasht with a book, and I read it for eleven days, and there is a king in it called Bahram who was a hunter, and when I came to the desk in New York and the man said name, I said Bahram.”
“You can’t just — ”
“You can. That is what America turns out to be.” He almost smiled. “You can do it once, at a desk, in eight seconds, and then it is done and there is nobody alive who can tell them otherwise.”

She thought about the ledger at the card table and a fountain pen and a line that said the undersigned certifies that all statements given upon entry are true, and she felt something go cold along her arms.
“Did you find him?” she said.
Bahram walked four or five steps.
“That,” he said, “is a different story and I am saving it.”

At six in the morning the horn went and they came off, and in the parts department Ida was going down the row with the small bottle, the night one, the one that put you down, and when she got to Alma she stopped.
“You been crying.”
“No.”
“Hon,” Ida said, “I been doing this eleven years and I can tell in the dark.” She poured out the little tin cup. “Drink that. And listen to me. Whatever he’s telling you out there — ”
“He’s telling me stories.”

“I know what he’s doing,” Ida said. “I seen it before. It works.” She capped the bottle. “You just remember there’s a fella with a microphone forty feet from here whose whole business is finding out what a person’s got and selling it back to ’em, and the only two people in this building he don’t know a thing about is you and the Sheik.”
Alma drank the cup.
“And Ida,” she said, “the two of us — how long do you give us?”
Ida looked at her a moment.
“Hon,” she said, “I don’t give anybody anything. Lie down.”
7. THE STORY SHE TELLS
She told him on the ninth night and it was the only time in eleven hundred hours that she started a conversation.

They were down to forty couples. The band was five men now — the second trumpet had gone back to Toledo — and Fitz was playing something with a lot of space in it, and the bleachers were maybe a third full because it was a Monday and it was raining.
“I want to tell you something,” Alma said, “and then I don’t want to talk about it again.”
“All right.”
“I mean it. Not once.”

“Then you should not tell me,” Bahram said. “Because if you tell me I will want to talk about it, and I will have to spend the next month not doing it, and I am already carrying as much as I can carry.”
“I have to tell somebody.”
He walked her four or five steps.
“Then tell me,” he said. “And I will not bring it up. That is a real promise and you may hold me to it.”
“I’m from Kentucky,” she said. “Harlan County. My daddy was in the mines and his daddy was in the mines and I got out at twenty-five, which where I’m from is not getting out, that’s running off.”
“Why did you run off?”

“Roy.” She said the name and it did nothing to her, which was interesting. “Roy Sutter. He came through with a road crew in ’27 and he had a way of standing that I liked and we were married in April and in Detroit by August, because they were paying five dollars a day at Ford’s and everybody in Harlan County had heard about it, and half of them came.”
“They were paying five dollars a day in 1927.”
“They were.”
“They were paying four in 1931,” Bahram said, “and then they were paying nobody. I was there for both ends of it.”
“We might have passed each other.”
“We did not,” he said. “The Rouge is the size of your county. I worked at a door for five years and I could not tell you what was behind the next building.”
“Ruth came in May of ’28,” Alma said.
That was the first time she’d said the name out loud since the summer and she had to walk a while before the next part.

“She was — ” and she found she had nothing. All the words for it were the same six words everybody used and none of them were the thing. “She had a way of holding a cup with both hands like it was heavy. Even when it wasn’t. Even at four. I don’t know where she got it.”
“Go on.”

“Roy was laid off in the spring of ’31 and then he got on again in the fall for eleven weeks and then that was it. And you know how that goes, you were there. He went out every morning for about a year.” She could hear the rain on the roof over the music. “He went to Toledo in February. He said there was something at Willys. He wrote once in March. There’s no letters after March.”
“You do not know if he is alive.”

“I don’t know if he’s alive.” She said it flatly. “And I’ll tell you the ugly part, which is that by June I’d stopped hoping he was, because if he was alive it meant he’d chosen, and I could carry the other thing better.”
Bahram made a small sound of understanding that had no words in it and she was grateful for it for the rest of her life.
“I was at the laundry on Vernor till May,” she said. “Then they cut to two girls. And then it was just — ”
She stopped.
“You do not have to.”

“I’m going to.” She got her breath. “It was July. It was the eleventh of July, it was a Monday, and I carried her there myself. I want you to know that. Whatever else, I carried her there myself and I didn’t let anybody else do it.”
“Where?”

“Out past Northville,” Alma said. “It’s a long way. I had a nickel for the streetcar as far as it goes and then it’s a walk. It was ninety-some degrees. She had on the blue dress with the smocking, because that was the good one, and I did her hair, and I remember thinking it was a stupid thing to be doing, doing a child’s hair on a day like that, and I did it anyway and I took my time over it.”
She heard her own voice going and let it go.

“There was a woman there. She was kind about it. They were all kind about it, that’s — that’s a thing nobody tells you, that everybody’s kind and it doesn’t touch it at all. And there was a form to sign, because there’s always a form.”
“Yes.”

“And then I couldn’t stay.” Alma’s hands had closed on the back of his shirt. “That’s the part. I want to say it out loud one time. I couldn’t stay. I got up and I walked out of that building and down that road and I did not look back at it, not once, not one time, because I knew if I looked back I wasn’t going to be able to do it, and so I have never seen — ”
She stopped.
Bahram walked her around the corner by the fire door and past the bandstand and around again, and did not say anything, and did not ask her to finish the sentence.
“So that’s July,” she said, when she could. “And that’s why I’m in a dance hall in Ecorse, Michigan.”
He waited a long time before he spoke, long enough that the band changed songs.
“What is the money for?”
“What?”

“The thousand dollars.” He said it gently. “Everyone in this building has a number. Chick and Dot want a boarding house, they told me on the second night. The boy from Wyandotte wants a truck. What is yours?”
“Does it matter?”
“It matters more than anything else about you,” Bahram said. “It is the only thing in here that is real. Everything else is what we tell each other at four in the morning.”
The rain got harder on the roof.
“A stone,” Alma said.
“A stone.”
“A headstone.” She looked at the maple going by under them. “They’re eleven dollars for the small kind, with a name on it. And a date. I priced it.”
“Eleven dollars.”
“Eleven dollars.”
“And the prize is one thousand.”
“Yes.”

He did not say the obvious thing. She had braced for it all through the sentence — then why are you here, Alma, for eleven dollars, for a piece of rock — and he did not say it, and she looked up at him and his jaw was set and he was staring at the far bleachers.
“All right,” he said.
“That’s it? All right?”
“You said you did not want to talk about it again.” Bahram took the corner. “So. All right.”
He kept that promise.

He never brought it up. Not in the sixth week when she was hallucinating and would have told him anything. Not at the end. Not once in eleven hundred hours did he ask her a single question about the eleventh of July, and at the time she thought it was the finest thing anybody had ever done for her.
Thirty-nine years later, in a room in Dearborn with a photograph on the wall, she would still be trying to work out whether it had been.
II. THE HORSES
8. HEEL AND TOE
The gate fell off in the second week and Doyle went to work.

Alma could read it in the bleachers before she could read it anywhere else. The first Saturday there had been nineteen hundred people. The second Saturday there were maybe eleven hundred, and on the Tuesday after that she counted three hundred and stopped counting.
The reason was simple and Doyle explained it to them himself, standing on the edge of the maple with the microphone down at his side, off, talking to the dancers like a foreman.

“You’re too good,” he said. “That’s the problem. Forty couples and every one of you looks like you could go another month. Nobody pays a quarter to watch forty healthy people take a walk.” He looked down the line. “So we’re going to start doing derbies. That’s a race. You’ll hate it. It’s how this works and I’d rather tell you than let you find out.”
The first one was a heel-and-toe.

The rule was that the toe of the back foot had to touch the heel of the front foot on every step, no gap, no running, and you went in a circle around the outside of the floor for one hour, and the last two couples to make each lap dropped out of the race and the rest kept going, and the couple standing at the end got twenty dollars in cash.
Twenty dollars. Doyle held it up in the air, four fives, and the room came alive for the first time in eight days.
“You do not have to win,” Bahram said, while they were lining up.
“Twenty dollars.”

“You do not have to win,” he said again. “Listen to me. There are forty couples. Doyle needs a spectacle and a spectacle needs somebody to break in front of everybody. If you decide to win this you will be that person, and you will be that person in front of a photographer, and then he will own you.” He shifted his grip on her hand. “We finish in the middle. Every time. That is the whole plan and it is the plan for six weeks.”
“Twenty dollars is — ”
“Twenty dollars is two weeks of your life,” Bahram said. “Do the sum properly.”
She did the sum properly. She hated it.
They finished eleventh out of forty and Chick and Dot Mullaly won, and the crowd went home happy, and it cost her the skin on both heels.

The derbies came every day after that and they were all different and they were all the same. Figure-eights, twenty-five laps. Elimination sprints for the men while the women stood at the rail and watched. Something Doyle called a dynamite sprint, which was three minutes of actual fast dancing and was worse than an hour of anything else.
And they ruined the storytelling.

That was what Alma noticed first, and she was ashamed of noticing it. Not her feet. Not the twelve pounds she’d lost. The fact that from the tenth day onward, the hours that had been for talking got eaten, because a derby left you unable to put a sentence together for two hours afterward, and by then it was cot call.
“We are losing it,” she said, on the eleventh night.
“I know.”
“You said you’d make it last. There isn’t going to be — ”
“I know, Alma.” He rubbed at his eyes with the back of his wrist. “I have been thinking about it for four days.”
The answer came at hour two hundred and seventy and it came from Doyle, who did not know he had given it.

They were in the middle of a heel-and-toe, ninth lap, and Doyle was calling it over the microphone — look at the Sheik, folks, look at the footwork on that fella — and there was nothing at all to look at, Bahram was doing the same shuffle as everybody else, but Doyle said it and the crowd looked, and something went across Bahram’s face that Alma had not seen before.
That night he stopped in the middle of the floor.
“Give me your hands.”
“What?”
“Both hands. Face me.” He took them. They were still moving — you had to be — but he had turned her so they were square on, chest to chest, hands joined, sliding sideways. “Now. There was a king.”
“Barney, I can’t — I’m not going to remember a — ”

“You are not going to remember it,” he said. “You are going to learn it. There is a difference and your legs know it and your head does not.” He pushed her left hand out and up, and she went with it, and they turned. “There was a king. He had everything. He had ruled for three hundred years and he had made — ”
He turned her under his arm, badly, and she stumbled, and he caught her.

“Again. He had made everything. Cloth. Medicine. Ships. Bricks. Every good thing in the world, he had thought of it.” He turned her again and this time she came around clean. “And after three hundred years he stood up in front of everybody and said: all of this is mine. I made it. There is nobody above me.”
“What happened to him?”
“That turn,” Bahram said, “is what happened to him.”
She did it again. Out, under, around. The light went across her face and away.

“That is the whole story,” he said. “That turn. When you do that turn you are Jamshid, and you are saying I did this myself, and everything he had came off him like a coat. His men left. His country left. He ran for a hundred years and they caught him in the end.” He stopped her. “Now. Show me.”
Alma did the turn.
“Again.”
She did it again.
“That is Jamshid,” Bahram said. “You have him now. You will have him in forty years. I could take the whole poem out of your head with a hammer and your arm would still know that.”
It became the method and it saved the book of it.

He blocked it out in pieces small enough to survive a derby. A step, a turn, a lift of the elbow, a way of setting the shoulders — and each one was a piece of the story, and he’d give her one in the good hours and then, in the ruined hours after a sprint when neither of them could speak, he would just do it, put her through the figure, and she’d come out the other side with the story sitting in her without a word having been said.

“It is not mine,” he said, when she told him it was clever. “This is how it was always done. Nobody read that poem for eight hundred years. There was a man in a coffee house with a stick and he acted it out. He did the voices. He did the fighting. That is what it is for.”
“So I’m the coffee house.”

“You are the coffee house,” Bahram agreed. “It is not a large coffee house and it has one customer and the customer is on the floor of an automobile showroom in Michigan.” He turned her under his arm. “But it is running. Which is more than can be said for the one my uncle had.”
Doyle noticed within four days.

He noticed because it was his job to notice and because a man with a microphone spends nine hours a day looking for the one thing in a room that is different. He started drifting past them. He started putting the crowd’s eye on them — and here’s the Sheik and Alma, folks, doing something fancy over here.
And Alma, who was twenty-nine years old and had not been looked at with approval by anybody in a year and a half, felt herself lift, and stood up straighter, and let it feel good.
“Don’t,” Bahram said.
“Don’t what?”
“That.” He was looking at the far bleachers. “He has found the thing about us. He will use it. From now on you should assume that anything he likes about us is a thing that is going to be taken.”
“You’re not a very cheerful man, Barney.”
“No,” he said, and turned her under his arm, and the crowd made a small pleased noise, and somewhere behind them Doyle Ferrin filed it away.
9. THE BLACKSMITH’S APRON
There was a man in the third row on the north side who came four nights a week and never brought anybody with him.

Alma noticed him around the twelfth day because he was the only person in the building who did not eat. Everybody in those bleachers ate — peanuts, sandwiches out of paper, Doyle sold hot dogs at intermission for a nickel — and this man sat with his hands on his knees and watched the floor and left when the lights came up.
He was maybe fifty. He wore a jacket that had been a good jacket. There was something wrong with his left hand; he kept it curled.
“That one has been here since the first week,” Bahram said.
“You’ve been watching him?”
“I have been watching everybody. There is nothing else to look at.” He turned them at the corner. “That man was at the Rouge.”
“How can you possibly — ”
“Because of the hand,” Bahram said, “and because of the way he does not spend money.”
The story came on the thirteenth night and it came because of the man in the third row.
They were doing the slow circle at half past one in the morning and Bahram said, without any lead-up:
“After Jamshid there was a king who had a snake on each shoulder.”
Alma laughed. She was too tired for it to come out as a laugh; it came out as a cough.
“You are going to have to do better than that.”

“I am not going to do better than that. That is the story.” He took her hands and squared her up. “His name was Zahhak. A devil kissed him on both shoulders and two black snakes grew out of the places, and they could not be cut off — cut one and two grow — and they had to be fed.”
“Fed what.”
“Brains,” Bahram said. “Two men a day. Every day. For a thousand years.”
She stopped laughing.

“That is the number in the poem. A thousand years. And it works, that is the horrible part, it is not a wicked king who is overthrown in a fortnight, he rules. He builds. There are roads. There are officials with ledgers.” He was walking her in the long slow circle now, keeping her square. “There is a man in every town whose job it is to bring the two names. And the country gets used to it. That is what the poem is actually about. Not the snakes. The getting used to it.”
Alma looked out at the bleachers, at the sixty or seventy people in them at half past one in the morning, and at the man in the third row on the north side with his hands on his knees.
“How does it end?”
“A blacksmith,” Bahram said.

“His name was Kaveh and he was nobody. He was not a prince, he had no army, he was a man who made nails. And he had eighteen sons and the snake king took seventeen of them, one at a time, over the years, and Kaveh said nothing, because what does a man who makes nails say.”
He turned her under his arm.
“And then they came for the eighteenth.”
The band was three men and the piano.

“So Kaveh went to the palace. And there is a thing they made him do — the king had a paper, and all the great men of the country had signed it, and it said that the king was a just king and that everyone was content.” Bahram’s voice had not changed at all and that was somehow the worst of it. “They put the paper in front of Kaveh and told him to sign, because they wanted a workingman on it. And he read it. And he tore it up in front of the whole court.”
“They killed him.”
“They gave him his son,” Bahram said. “That is what happened. He tore up the paper and shouted at the king and they were so astonished that they gave him the boy and let them both walk out.”
“That’s not — ”

“It is not the end. He walked out into the street with his son and he took off the leather apron he wore at the forge — the thing he wore to keep the sparks off, it was filthy, it was a rag — and he put it up on a spear.”
Alma had stopped moving her feet properly and he corrected her with his knee.

“And that was the flag,” Bahram said. “That was the flag of the country for a thousand years afterward. Kings put jewels on it. It was carried into every battle in the poem. And it was a blacksmith’s dirty apron and everyone knew it was a blacksmith’s dirty apron and that was the entire point of it.”
He said the last of it a little louder than he needed to.

Not much. Not so that anybody would have called it shouting. But the man in the third row on the north side had turned his head, and was watching them, and Alma understood with a small cold shock that Bahram had known he was there and had been telling it to him.
They went around twice more.
“March,” the man said.
His voice carried. There were sixty people in that room and no crowd noise to swallow it.
Bahram stopped them.
“March,” the man said again. “The seventh of March. Were you there.”
“No,” Bahram said. “I had been laid off fourteen months. I read it in the paper like everybody else.”

“I was there.” The man turned the curled hand over in his lap and looked at it. “Three thousand of us walked out to the Dearborn line to ask them for work. That’s all it was. Ask. And they had the fire hoses on us at the bridge and it was twenty degrees, and then they started shooting, and they killed four boys, and the oldest one of ’em was twenty-five.”
Nobody in the bleachers moved.
“They shot ’em in the back,” the man said. “And I’ve been out of work since the twenty-ninth of April and I come here four nights a week because I can’t stand to be in the house.”
Alma did not know what to do with her face.
Bahram let a moment go by. Then he said, evenly, across forty feet of empty maple:
“Then you already know the story. I have only been telling you the old version.”
The man looked at him for a long time.
“Fella,” he said, “what’s your actual name?”
And Bahram told him.

The man tried it. He got it wrong the first time and Bahram corrected him and he got it on the second, roughly, badly, but he got it — the first American mouth to hold it in eight years — and he nodded once and sat back and put his hands on his knees.
He was there on the Thursday and the Friday. On the Saturday he wasn’t, and he never came again, and Alma looked for him at the end and he was not in the room.
Doyle had been standing at the edge of the bandstand for the last of it with the microphone off.
He came over at the horn.
“That was good,” he said.
Neither of them answered.

“No, I mean it. That was good.” He was not being sarcastic. That was the thing about him she could never get past — he was never sarcastic. “The snakes and the fella with the apron. Where’s that from?”
“It is a poem.”
“Huh.” Doyle nodded, thinking. “Could you do that up there?” He pointed at the microphone stand with his chin. “In front of the house. On a Saturday.”
“No.”
“Twenty dollars.”
“No,” Bahram said.
Doyle grinned at him with the whole of his face, entirely without malice, the way a man grins at a fish that has just gone off the hook and is still in the water and is not going anywhere.
“Okay,” he said. “Sure. Not tonight.”
10. TWELVE MEALS A DAY

The food came on tin trays through a hatch in the wall of the old parts department and it came twelve times in every twenty-four hours and it never stopped and by the third week it had become the most important thing in Alma’s life.

Not because she was hungry. She had stopped being hungry around the two hundredth hour, which the doctor said was normal and which she did not believe. It was that the meals were the only thing that changed. The dancing did not change. The horn did not change. But at some hours there were eggs and at some hours there was the stew, and so the eggs and the stew became weather, and she found herself, at twenty-nine years old, in the fourth year of a national catastrophe, on a maple floor, lying in wait for scrambled eggs.
Bahram had a running quarrel with all of it.
“I want to say something about the bread.”
“Say it.”

“It is not bread.” He was holding a slice of it in the hand that wasn’t on her back, eating it in the small fast bites that were the only way to eat while moving. “It is a kind of white pillow. It has no argument in it.”
“It’s bread, Barney.”

“Bread has a crust that fights you,” he said. “That is the purpose of a crust. This surrenders.” He ate the rest of it. “I would like to be clear that I am going to eat every piece of it that this man gives me.”
“I know.”
“I am reporting. I am not complaining.”
“You keep saying that.”
“Because there is a difference,” Bahram said, “and I am the only person in this building who observes it.”
The list of grievances grew and she began to keep it, mentally, for entertainment, the way you’d keep a bird list.

The coffee, which he said was brown water pretending to a career. The pie, which he had opinions about that took eleven minutes to deliver. Cheese — he had a whole thing about American cheese that started reasonably and ended with him saying that a nation that would do that to milk would do it to anything, and Alma had to put her forehead on his shoulder because she was laughing and couldn’t be seen to.
And the tea.
The tea was the real one. She learned not to bring it up.
“They put it in a bag.”
“Barney.”
“They put the leaves in a little cloth bag,” Bahram said, “and they hang it in the water like a drowned mouse, and then they take it out and throw it away, and then — then — they put milk in it.”
“Everybody puts milk in it.”
“My mother would have shut the door of the house.”
Chick Mullaly took a liking to him, which was not something either of them had planned.

Chick and Dot were the professionals — they’d done four contests that year, Wheeling and Louisville and two in Ohio, and they arrived at the Rialto with their own shoes and their own foot powder and a way of moving that made everything Alma did look like an accident. Dot could sleep on her feet for eleven minutes at a stretch. Chick had a face like a closed shop.
But he liked Bahram, and it was because of the complaining.
“Do the cheese one,” he’d say, coming past on the outside.
“I am not a vaudeville.”
“Do the cheese one for Dot. She ain’t heard it.”

And Bahram would sigh in a way that took about four seconds and then do the cheese one, and Dot would laugh in her sleep-walking half-conscious way, and the four of them would go around the floor in a loose group at three in the morning like the last people at a party.
It was Chick who explained the trays.
“You know why it’s twelve, right?”
“Because they are generous,” Bahram said.

“Because you can’t quit on a full stomach.” Chick said it without any particular feeling. “Fella gets hungry, he starts thinking about his mother’s kitchen, and then he’s out the door in an hour. Ferrin knows that. Every promoter knows that. It’s the cheapest thing they do.” He shrugged. “Best food I’ve had in two years, and I’ve had it in nine states, and every plate of it’s a nail.”
Alma’s own education went the other way and she was, she would admit later, a slower student.
She had thought Persia was near Egypt. She said so out loud on the fourteenth day and there was a silence of a quality she had not previously experienced.
“Egypt,” Bahram said.
“I don’t know! It’s — it’s all — ”
“Finish the sentence.”
“It’s all over there,” Alma said, “and I’m from Harlan County, Kentucky, and I’ve been to Detroit and once to Cincinnati, and I’m not going to apologize for it.”
And Bahram laughed. Properly, out loud, head back — the only time she heard him do it in the whole first thousand hours — and he laughed so long that a judge came over to see if something was wrong.
“That,” he said, when he could, “is the first honest thing anyone in this country has ever said to me about it.”
“Well, where is it?”

“Two thousand miles from Egypt. Further than you are from Mexico.” He steered them past the stage. “There is a sea between us and them and a desert on the other side and a different alphabet and a different language and a different religion for two thousand years before theirs. And I want to be fair — I could not find Kentucky on a map in 1924. I thought all of America was flat.”
“It’s not flat.”
“I have since learned that it is not flat,” he said gravely.
They arrived, over about a week, at the deal.

She would call him Barney out on the floor, because everybody did, because the alternative was a small war every hour with a man on a microphone. And off the floor — in the parts department, in the fifteen, at the hatch, in the dark where nobody was selling anything — she would use his name.
She practiced it. She was bad at it for four days and then she had it.
“Say it again,” he said, the first time she got it clean.
She said it again.
“Once more.”
“Barney — ”
“Once more, please.”
She said it a third time.
“Thank you,” Bahram said, and did not explain, and got up at the horn and went out and answered to Barney for nine hours.
11. MOCK WEDDING
Doyle announced it on a Thursday for the following Saturday and he put it on handbills all over Wyandotte and Lincoln Park and River Rouge.
SEE THEM MARRIED ON THE FLOOR!
THE FIRST MARATHON WEDDING IN MICHIGAN
SAT. NITE — 25¢ — DOYLE FERRIN PRESENTS

The couple were nineteen and twenty-one and their names were Vern and Bernice and they had come in from Trenton with two dollars between them. They had not been engaged. They had known each other four weeks, three of them on that floor.
Doyle had offered them fifty dollars.
“They cannot be serious.”
“They took the money,” Alma said.

“Yes. Of course they took the money.” Bahram was walking her hard, faster than the tempo, which he did when he was upset and denied doing. “That is not the part. Do they understand that it will be real?”
“It’s not real. It’s a stunt.”
“There is a minister coming.”
“He’s a — ” Alma had heard this from Ida. “He’s a real minister, but there’s no license. Doyle’s not paying for a license. It’s a show.”
Bahram stopped dead in the middle of the floor, which you were not supposed to do, and a judge’s head came around.
“Then it is worse,” he said.
She could not get him past it and it took the better part of two days to understand why, and when she did understand it she was ashamed of how long it had taken.

“It is not the money,” he said, at four in the morning. “Everybody in this building is doing it for money and I would be a hypocrite. It is that they will stand in front of a man of God in front of a paying crowd and say the words, and then it will not have happened.”
“That’s the joke of it. That’s the point.”

“Yes.” He walked her around. “Where I am from, a wedding is three days. It is not an afternoon, it is three days, and half the town is in it, and there are things that must be said by the bride’s people and things that must be said by the groom’s, and there is a moment — ” He stopped. “There is a moment when they hold a cloth over the two of them and rub two loaves of sugar together above it, so that the life will be sweet. Somebody’s aunt does it. It is always somebody’s aunt.”
Alma had never heard him describe anything from home that was not either a mountain or a grievance.
“And?”
“And I will never have it,” Bahram said.
The band was two men.

“There is no one to hold the cloth,” he said. “There is no aunt. There is nobody in this hemisphere who would know what to do, and by the time I am dead there will be nobody anywhere who remembers that I was supposed to have it. So.” He took the corner. “So it is difficult to watch two children in Michigan throw it in the street for fifty dollars, and I am aware that this is not their fault, and I am aware that I am being unbearable.”
“You’re not being unbearable.”
“I am being unbearable,” he said, “but thank you.”
The Saturday drew fourteen hundred people, which was the best gate since the first weekend.

They cleared a space in the middle of the maple and the remaining thirty-six couples went around the outside of it in a slow ring, still moving, because nobody was excused, and Vern and Bernice stood in the middle and did not stop moving either — they swayed the whole way through it, side to side, because a judge was eleven feet away.
Fitz played the wedding march on the piano with a lot of vibrato.

Bernice had a veil made of cheesecloth and a bunch of yellow flowers that Ida had got from somewhere. She was crying before the minister opened his mouth and she cried all the way through it and Alma could not tell from any distance whether it was joy or exhaustion or the plain animal fact of ninety-one hours without sleep, and thought, going around the ring with her head on Bahram’s shoulder, that probably Bernice couldn’t have told her either.

The minister was a real minister. He was about sixty and he had a bad cold and he said the words correctly and gravely and did not play to the crowd once. When he got to for richer for poorer the whole building made a noise, and he waited it out with his eyes shut.
They said it. Both of them. They said all of it.
And then Doyle Ferrin came out on the maple with the microphone and put one hand on Vern’s shoulder and one hand on Bernice’s and said:
“Folks — the first married couple in the history of the Rialto!”
And fourteen hundred people stood up, and the band went into something fast, and the silver started coming down.

That was the other thing. Doyle had told the crowd to bring change. The coins came out of the bleachers and hit the maple and rolled, and Vern went down on his knees to pick them up — on his knees, which was a disqualification, and Doyle waved the judge off, which was the only time Alma ever saw a rule bent in that building — and Bernice stood in the middle of it in a cheesecloth veil with her hands over her face.
Eleven dollars and some, Ida said afterward. Plus the fifty.

They went out in the fifth week. Bernice’s ankle turned during a figure-eight and Vern took her down with him, and Doyle gave them a beautiful send-off, and the band played their verse, and the crowd sang along.

Alma never found out what happened to them. She looked, once, in 1938, in a telephone directory in a public library, for a Vern and Bernice in Trenton, Michigan, and there was nothing, and she closed the book and did not look again.
“Do you want to know the worst thing?” Bahram said, that Saturday night, after the crowd had gone and the coins were swept up.
“There’s a worse thing?”

“They will be married,” he said. “Not on paper. But they will believe it, because they said it out loud in front of a minister and a thousand people, and in ten years they will not be able to remember that it was not real. That is how it works. You say a thing in front of enough people and it becomes true whether or not anyone has written it down.”
He turned her at the corner.
“That is the most dangerous thing I know about this country,” he said, “and I have been trying to explain it to myself for eight years, and tonight I finally saw it done properly.”
12. ZOMBIE TREADMILL
Ida changed the bottle in the third week and did not mention it.

Alma knew because of the licorice. The licorice had always been on top of something and now the something had come up through it, a flat metal taste at the back of the tongue that stayed for an hour, and the warmth that used to come twenty minutes after arrived in four.
“This is different.”
“It’s the same bottle, hon.”
“Ida.”
Ida looked at her for a second and a half.

“It’s stronger,” she said. “There’s twenty-nine couples left and Ferrin wants eight by the end of the month and a person can’t do that on beef stew.” She capped it. “You want the old one, I’ll give you the old one, and you’ll be out by Friday.”
Alma drank it.
The sounds went first.

That was the part nobody had warned her about and the part she could never afterward describe to anyone in a way that made sense. It was not that things got louder. It was that they stopped being sounds and started being touch.
The cymbal became a thing that landed on the skin of her face.

The air horn — the air horn stopped being possible. She would stand in the last minute of the forty-five with her whole body braced against a thing that had not happened yet, and when it came it went through her like a hand pushing her chest, and twice she found she had put her arms up.
“It is the bottle,” Bahram said.
“It’s not the bottle.”
“Alma. It is the bottle.”
“Then why aren’t you — ”

“I am,” he said. “I have been for four days. The lights have edges on them. There is a green line around Doyle.” He turned her at the corner. “I did not tell you because I was hoping I was the only one, and if that seems stupid to you, I agree.”
The zombie treadmill was on the eighteenth day.

Doyle explained it to the crowd with real pleasure. The couples were blindfolded — actual cloth, tied around the eyes — and then bound together at the wrist with a leather strap, and then they raced. Twenty-five laps of the outside of the floor, blind, roped, at speed.
Alma stood at the rail while Ida tied the cloth and understood that she was frightened in a way she had not been since July.
“Don’t fight it,” Chick said, going past. “Fella that fights it goes into the bleachers. Just let your feet do it. Your feet know the room.”
The horn.
Here is what she could remember of it afterward, which was not much and was not in order.

The floor was longer than the room. She knew the room was ninety feet and the floor under her went on for a great deal more than ninety feet and there was no contradiction in it at all; it simply was.
The crowd was above her and also below her.
There was a bird.

It was in the roof. It was in the girders over the bandstand and its wings went out past the walls of the building on both sides and it was made of gold and blue in flat pieces like a window in a church, and it was not frightening. That was the thing she came back to for the next forty years. She had never in her life seen anything less frightening. She was blindfolded and roped to a man and running, and there was an enormous bird in the ceiling of an automobile showroom in Ecorse, Michigan, and she felt about it exactly the way you feel when somebody sits down next to your bed.
She was crying inside the blindfold before the tenth lap and she did not know it until it got to her chin.
They came thirteenth. Somebody went into the bleachers on the eighth lap and it was not them.
“There was a bird,” she said, in the parts department, with the cloth still in her hand.
Bahram was sitting on the edge of the men’s cot with his head down between his knees and it took him a long moment to lift it.
“What?”
“In the roof. A bird.” She was shaking. “Barney, I’m going out of my mind.”
“No.”
“There was a bird — ”
