“Alma.” He got up and came around the end of the canvas, which was not allowed. “Listen to me. What did it look like.”
“Gold. And blue. Like — like a window.”
He sat down on the floor next to her cot with his back against the wall.
“All right,” he said. “Then I have to tell you about Zal, and I am going to do it now, out of order, and badly, because we have nine minutes.”
“There was a baby born in the mountains,” he said, “and his hair was white.”
“White.”

“Snow white, from the day he came out. His father was a great man and he looked at that child and he was ashamed of him. He thought it was a curse or a devil’s child or a punishment, and he could not bear that the country would see it.” Bahram had his eyes shut. “So he took the baby up onto a mountain and he left it on the rock. To die. Because it was easier than being looked at.”
Alma had gone very still.

“And there was a bird,” Bahram said. “She is called the Simorgh. She is old — she is older than everything, she has seen the world burn three times — and she nests on that mountain, and she came down to take the baby to feed her own young. And she picked him up. And she looked at him.”
“And?”

“And she did not eat him. She took him back up to the nest and she raised him. For years. She fed him and she taught him to speak and she kept him warm under her wing, and he grew up in a nest on a rock with birds, and he did not know he was a man.”
The horn was going to go in three minutes. She could feel it coming the way you feel a train.

“His father dreamed about him,” Bahram said, “years later, when he was old. And he went up the mountain, and he stood at the bottom of the rock and called, and the Simorgh looked at the boy — who was grown by then, a young man with white hair, who could speak the language of birds — and she said: there is your father. He has come for you. You may go.”
“Did he go?”

“He went.” Bahram opened his eyes. “That is the part nobody can ever explain. He went. She gave him a feather and she said, if you ever need me, burn this and I will come, and he walked down the mountain to the man who left him on it, and he never once, in the whole rest of the poem, said a word about it.”
Alma sat on a cot in a parts department with a blindfold in her fist.
“Why are you telling me this.”

“Because you saw her,” Bahram said, “and I did not want you to spend one hour thinking you were mad. You are not mad. You are a person who has not slept in eighteen days and something in you went and found the biggest thing I ever gave you and put it in the roof.”
“Barney — ”
“And because the story is not about a bird,” he said. “It is about a man who left a child on a rock because he could not bear to be looked at, and then lived to be old, and dreamed.”
She said nothing at all.
The horn went off, and went through her chest like a hand, and they got up and went out and walked.
13. THE HORSE
It happened at half past three in the morning on the nineteenth day and it took eleven seconds.

Alma had gone out at cot call to find Ida, because the arch of her right foot had started doing something she needed a name for, and Ida was not in the parts department, and the light was on over the card table in the little office that used to be where they wrote up the finance on a Studebaker.
The door was open four inches.
Doyle was at the desk with the ledger. Bahram was standing in front of it.

Doyle counted bills off a roll — she could see his thumb doing it, three, four, five — and put them on the desk and turned them around, and Bahram picked them up and folded them once and put them in his trouser pocket.
Neither of them said anything. That was the part. There was no conversation. It was the eleven-second transaction of two men who had done it before and had nothing left to arrange.
Then Doyle said, “Same Friday,” and Bahram said, “Yes,” and Alma got herself back around the corner of the corridor before the door moved.

She lay on the cot for the rest of the fifteen with her eyes open and her heart going like a bird in a box, and she did the arithmetic, and the arithmetic came out clean the first time, which was how she knew she had been stupid for nineteen days.
A man who knew to slide his feet on the first night. A man told me at the door. He was very sure.
A man who knew, on day one, that the arch comes down. That you would want the cot in the light. That the fifteen minutes would start being stolen from you.
A man who had never done this before.

A man who said, on the very first night, in front of nineteen hundred people, not one word from that man is going to be true — and who was, at that moment, on the payroll of that man, and had been since before she walked in the door.

They had not been matched. She had stood in a line in a green dress and Doyle Ferrin had walked down the row of men and put his hand on one and moved on and stopped at the third, and she had thought that was chance, and it was staging. It was the oldest staging there was. Chick had told her about it himself in the second week and she had listened to it as a story about other people.
They’ll run a horse or two. Fella that knows the racket. Ferrin’s got ’em in every town.
The horn went off and she got up and walked out onto the maple and put her hand in his.
She did not say anything for eleven hours.

That is not a figure of speech. She counted them later off the board, because she wanted to know, and it was eleven hours and about twenty minutes, from the half past three until nearly three in the afternoon, and in all that time she did not speak one word to him.
He knew inside of ten minutes. She felt him find out — a change in the hand on her back — and then she felt him decide not to ask.
So he talked.

He talked the entire eleven hours. He talked through four meals and a heel-and-toe derby and the whole grey hollow middle of a Wednesday morning when the bleachers were empty and the band was Fitz alone and the room smelled of the mop. He told her about the three brothers who divided the world and the youngest one, Iraj, who got the best of it and gave it back and was murdered by the other two anyway. He told her about a man in Constantinople who painted numbers on buses and had opinions about the numeral seven. He told her about the day the Rouge went to four dollars and what the line sounded like when the word came down it.

And every time she went — every time her head came down on his shoulder and her eyes went — she came back up somewhere else on the floor with his voice still going, unbroken, in the middle of a sentence, holding the place.
He did not once ask her what was wrong.
At three in the afternoon on the twentieth day she said:
“I saw Doyle pay you.”
Bahram walked her four steps.
“Yes,” he said.
“That’s it?”
“You asked me a question that was not a question.” He took the corner. “Ask me the real one.”
“How long.”

“Since the second of September. Twenty-two days before it opened.” His voice had nothing in it. “He was hiring in a room over a hardware store on Fort Street and there were sixty men there, and he took four of us.”
“To do what.”

“To last.” Bahram said it simply. “That is the whole job. He needs a floor that does not empty out in ten days. So he pays men who know how to stand up, and they stand up, and it looks like a contest. Chick and Dot are on it. There is a man called Prescott on it who went out in the second week because Doyle told him to.”
Alma’s mouth was very dry.
“And me,” she said.
“You are not on it.”
“I mean — was I part of it. The pairing.”
“Yes.”
She stopped.
“Keep walking,” Bahram said, “or a judge comes.”
She kept walking.
“He walked down that line and he had already chosen,” she said.
“He had chosen before he came out of the office.” Bahram’s jaw was tight. “He gave me a number in the afternoon. Number sixty-three. I did not know your name until he said it.”
“Why me?”

“I did not ask,” Bahram said. “I want to be exactly truthful with you and that is the truthful answer. I did not ask him why, because I had eleven dollars and I did not want to hear anything that would make it harder to take the job.”
They went around the floor twice.
“How much,” she said.
“Five dollars a week.”
“Five — ” She laughed, and it came out wrong, and a judge looked over. “Five dollars a week. To sell me.”

“To stand up,” Bahram said. “I want to be precise about what I was paid for, because it is the only thing I have. He paid me to stay on this floor. He did not pay me to lie to you. He did not pay me for anything I have said to you in nineteen days and he has never once asked me what we talk about.” He turned them at the corner. “And I have not told him one word. Not one. He has asked me twice and I have said nothing both times, and if you want to know what I have been buying with five dollars a week, that is it, and I would like it entered in the record.”
“You should have told me.”
“Yes.”
“On the first night. You should have — you stood there and you told me he’d lie to me — ”
“Yes,” Bahram said.
“Why didn’t you?”
And he said, after a long moment, and this was the sentence she took out and looked at for the next thirty-nine years:

“Because you were the only person in Michigan who did not already know something about me that was not true, and I wanted one more day of it. And then I wanted one more day of it. And then it was nineteen days and it had become a thing I had done rather than a thing I had not said.”
Doyle came past at the horn with the microphone off.
“Everything all right over here?”
“Yes,” Alma said.
Doyle looked at her, then at Bahram, then back at her, and he had the pleasantest face she had ever seen on a man.
“Good,” he said. “Because I got something planned for you two.”
14. THE COT IN THE LIGHT
What Doyle had planned was that they were going to be leaders.

He announced it on the Friday. Twenty-six couples left, and the judges had made their selection, and from tonight the eight best would take their fifteen minutes out on the maple in front of the house, under the spotlight, on the iron cots, where the people who had paid a quarter could watch them sleep.
Number sixty-three was on the list.
Alma stood at the rail and heard her own number and felt her whole body come up off the floor with relief.

That was the thing. That was the thing she could not get over, standing there — that a man had bought her partner before she’d ever walked in the building, and had chosen her off a card in a ledger for reasons she still did not know, and had been building something out of the two of them for three weeks, and had now decided to put her body on public display for fifteen minutes an hour — and her entire animal self had risen up in that moment and said thank God, I can lie down.
Bahram had told her this would happen on the second night.
He did not say anything about it now. She checked his face for it and there was nothing there, and she was so grateful for the nothing that she nearly said his name out loud in front of everybody.
She had not forgiven him. She wanted that on the record too.
They had had one more conversation about it, on the Thursday, and it had been short.
“Are you going to stop?”
“Taking his money?” Bahram considered it. “No.”
“No?”

“If I give it back he replaces me,” he said. “There are three other men on that payroll and he does not need four. And if he replaces me, he replaces me tomorrow, and you are paired with a stranger at hour four hundred, and you will not survive that. Neither would I.” He turned them at the corner. “So no. I am going to keep taking five dollars a week from a man I dislike in order to remain the person holding you up. If there is a clean way to do that I have not found it in three days of looking.”
And that was the entire trouble with him, she thought, and it was going to be the trouble with him right to the end: he was never once wrong, and it never once helped.
The cots came out at midnight.

There is no describing it and she tried for years. You are given, at last, the thing you have wanted more than food — a flat surface, and permission — and it is set down in the middle of a maple floor under a spotlight in front of six hundred people, and a man says your name into a microphone while you lie down on it.
You lie down anyway.

That was the discovery. She went down onto the canvas and it did not matter at all that they were watching. She had thought, standing at the rail, that she would feel it. She felt nothing. Somebody applauded. Somebody said something and somebody else laughed, and Doyle worked the house — there she is, folks, that’s number sixty-three, she’s been on her feet since the twenty-fourth of September — and Alma Sutter lay on an iron cot in a green dress in a cone of white light and was asleep in under nine seconds.
The shame came later. It came in the fifteen after, and it was not about being looked at.

It was that when the horn went, she had cried out. Out loud. In front of them. She heard herself do it as she came up, an animal noise of pure grief at being made to stand, and she got up and she saw a woman in the second row put her hand over her mouth, and Alma understood exactly what that woman had come for and exactly what she had just been given for twenty-five cents.
“You are going to want to tell me it is not so bad,” she said, later.
“I am not going to tell you that.”
“Good.”
“It is worse than everything else in this building,” Bahram said. “It is worse than the derbies. The derbies only take your legs.”
He walked her past the bandstand.

“I have been trying to think of what it is,” he said, “and I have got as far as this. In the poem there is a thing that happens to kings when they turn bad. There is a light on them — every king has it, it is how you know he is the real one, it comes down on him from God and it sits on him like a — ” he made a small helpless gesture with the hand on her back “ — I do not have the word. A brightness. And when a king does the unforgivable thing, it goes out of him, and everyone can see it go, and after that he is just a man in a room.”
“And?”

“And that is the opposite,” Bahram said. “That is what I keep coming back to at four in the morning. It comes on you and it means you are finished. Doyle puts the light on the ones he has decided are ready to be watched coming apart.” He shook his head slightly. “It is the same light, Alma. It is exactly the same light. It has only been turned around.”
Her right foot went on the twentieth day.

Not dramatically. There was no moment. She stepped down onto it in the second hour after a figure-eight derby and something in the middle of it did not answer, and she went sideways and he had her before her knee got anywhere near the maple, and nobody saw.
“Ida,” she said, in the fifteen.
Ida knelt down on the parts department floor and took the shoe off and put both thumbs into the arch and Alma made a sound.
“Mm,” Ida said.
“What’s mm.”
“It’s coming down.” She turned the foot in the light. “It’s not gone. It’s coming.”
“How long have I got.”

“Hon,” Ida said, “I ain’t going to tell you that, because you’ll spend it.” She put the shoe back on and laced it tight, tighter than Alma would have, and tied it off. “Two things. You keep that shoe on from here to the end, waking and sleeping, and I mean the end, whatever end that is. You take it off and the swelling comes up and it don’t go back in.”
“And the other thing?”
Ida stood up with a hand on the cot and her knees cracking.
“Don’t tell the Sheik,” she said. “He’ll carry you. And then it’ll be his feet too, and then there ain’t nobody left standing.”
Alma looked up at her.
“Ida,” she said. “How many of these have you done?”
“Eleven years.”
“And how many of them end all right?”
Ida picked up her bottles.
“Get your fifteen,” she said.

They put them on the cots in the light every night after that, and every night the crowd was a little smaller, and on the fourteenth night of October, which was a Friday, Alma lay down under the spotlight at eleven o’clock and slept for eleven minutes and dreamed about nothing at all.
15. FIVE HUNDRED
Sonny hung the five and the double naught on the Saturday afternoon and Doyle made a small ceremony of it.

Five hundred hours. Twenty days and twenty hours. Doyle had the band play a fanfare and got the four hundred people in the bleachers to count it down out loud from ten while the boy went up the ladder, and then he had the twenty-two remaining couples stand in a line at the rail — still moving, side to side, always side to side — and he went along the line saying their numbers and where they were from, and the crowd gave each one a hand.
“Number sixty-three,” Doyle said. “Alma Sutter, Harlan County, Kentucky, by way of Beaufait Street. And her partner. Folks — the Sheik of Ecorse.”
The applause was warm. There were people in that room who had been there four nights a week for three weeks.
Alma smiled and raised a hand and did not hear any of it, because at that moment her entire being was concentrated on the middle of her right foot.
It had started at about four that morning and by noon it was the only thing in the world.

The arch had come down. Not all at once, not with a sound, the way she had somehow expected — it had simply gone on going down, the way a roof goes down, over hours, and at some point in the small hours of the morning of the fifteenth of October the thing that had been holding the middle of her foot up had stopped doing it, and now every step put the whole of her weight through a place that had never been built to take weight.
It felt like standing on a hot stone.
It felt, at other moments, like standing on a stone that was inside the foot rather than under it.
Ida had a name for none of it. Ida knelt down at the four o’clock, and looked, and did not put her thumbs in this time, and said, “Well.”
“Well what.”
“Well, it’s down.”
“What do I do?”
“You keep the shoe on,” Ida said. “And you shift it. You put more on the left. And in about four days the left one’s going to start, and then you shift it back, and that’s how it goes till the end.”
“Ida — ”
“Hon, I’d lie to you if I thought it’d help,” Ida said, and got up.
She did not tell him. She had promised Ida and she kept it, and it lasted about nine hours, which she thought later was a fairly good showing.

He found out at the one o’clock in the morning because she went down at the corner by the fire door and this time it was not a lean, it was a drop, and he got both arms under her and it was not eight seconds, it was closer to forty, and a judge saw the whole thing and stood there with his hands behind his back and watched and did not call it, and Alma could never work out why.
“How long,” Bahram said, when she was upright.
“Since four.”
“This morning?”
“Yes.”
He said something in his own language, one word, short, and it was the only time in eleven hundred hours she ever heard him do it.
“Which foot.”
“Right.”
He steered her over to the outside line and put himself on her right side, and from that hour to the end of the contest he never once walked on her left again.
They found a way to do it inside a night.

He took her weight on the turns. That was the main thing. She would come round on the bad foot and there would be a hand under her elbow lifting about a third of her off the maple for the half-second it took, and it was so small that she doubted a judge four feet away could have named it.
They shortened the stride.

And they invented, between them, in the small hours of the fifteenth of October, a thing they never gave a name to, in which he would say Jamshid and she would do the turn — out, under, around — because the turn came off the ball of the foot and not the arch, and it bought her three or four steps of relief, and by the end of that night she was doing it thirty times an hour.
“You are going to wear that story out,” he said.
“It’s the only one that doesn’t hurt.”
“Then it is the right one,” Bahram said. “You may have it. It was never mine anyway.”
Nothing else happened on the fifteenth of October.
That was the truth of it and she went over it a great many times afterward, over years, looking for something in it, and there was nothing.

The gate was four hundred at the matinée and six hundred at night. There was a figure-eight derby at seven and they came out fourteenth. A couple from Ypsilanti went out at ten past nine when the woman’s shoulder came out of the socket during a turn, and Doyle gave them a beautiful send-off, and the band played, and the crowd sang, and Doyle wrote their verse on a cigarette paper on the corner of the bandstand:
I saw my mother in the second row,
I saw a bird as wide as Ohio,
I’d tell you the rest but I got to go —
So hold me up till the horn.

Alma heard it for the first time at half past ten on the night of the fifteenth of October, standing on a foot that had come down that morning, and she thought: he saw one too, then. And she looked for the man from Ypsilanti to ask him about the bird, and he had already gone out the door.
The cots came out at midnight. She was on them, in the light, and she slept eleven minutes.
At two in the morning she ate a plate of eggs standing up.

At four she was awake enough to be walked, and Bahram was telling her something about a horse — that Rostam’s horse had to be chosen out of an entire kingdom of horses and that he had tested every one by pressing his hand down on its back, and every horse in Persia went down under the hand, hundreds of them, one after another, for years, until at last there was one that stood.
“How long did that take him?”
“The poem does not say. Years.”
“Every horse in the country.”
“Every horse in the country,” Bahram said, “and I want you to understand that this is not a story about a horse. It is a story about how long a man will go on putting his hand down.”
At six they gave them coffee. At seven the mop came out.

At eight in the morning of the sixteenth of October, Sonny came up the ladder and took down the double naught and hung up a one and a six, and the day went on, and the crowd came in at noon, and the twenty-two couples that were left kept moving.
III. SILVER SHOWER
16. SILVER SHOWER
Doyle came to her with it on a Tuesday, alone, without the microphone.
“Twenty-two couples,” he said. “Six hundred hours Wednesday. And I got two hundred people in that house on a weeknight and I’m paying a band.”
“That’s not my trouble.”

“It’s everybody’s trouble, sweetheart, that’s the beauty of it.” He said it pleasantly. He was leaning on the rail while she went past and he timed the sentences to her circuits, picking up where he’d left off each time she came round, which took a kind of skill she had to admire. “I want to run a silver shower Saturday.”
“I don’t know what that is.”

“Sure you do. You’ve seen it.” He nodded at the bleachers. “I put a couple up front. I hand ’em the mic. They tell the folks about themselves — where they’re from, what brung ’em here, the hard part. And the folks throw change on the floor. And whatever lands, they keep.”
Alma went around.
“How much does it land,” she said, when she came back.
“Bernice and Vern got eleven dollars.”
“Eleven dollars.”
“That was a wedding,” Doyle said. “That’s the ceiling.” He straightened off the rail. “Think about it. I’ll ask the Sheik too but he’ll say no. He says no to everything and then he does it.”
Bahram said no.
“He’ll come back,” Alma said.

“He will come back on Friday and he will offer money,” Bahram agreed. “And I will say no on Friday as well, and then he will find another way, because a man like that does not go through a wall, he goes around it, and he has three weeks.”
“He said you’d say no and then do it.”
Bahram was quiet for a step or two.
“Did he,” he said.
She did it on the Saturday and she did not tell him beforehand.

That was deliberate. She sat with it through the whole of Friday and she worked out, quite coldly, that if she told him he would argue, and that he would be right, and that she would then have to either lose the argument or go against him having lost it, and both of those were more expensive than simply walking out onto the maple on a Saturday night and taking the microphone out of Doyle Ferrin’s hand.
Eight hundred people. Best gate in nine days.
“Number sixty-three,” Doyle said. “Alma Sutter.”

And he gave her the microphone and stepped back, and the band went quiet, and she stood in the middle of a maple floor moving side to side because a judge was watching, holding a live microphone, in front of eight hundred people, with her right arch flat and her hands shaking.
She had planned to tell them about Harlan County.

That was what she had decided in the small hours, that she would tell them about the mines and about Roy and about coming north for five dollars a day, and she opened her mouth to do it and what came out was:
“There was a boy.”
The room went very still.
She would think about that first sentence for the rest of her life — where it came from, why it came, whether some part of her had planned it and not told the rest. She was never able to decide.

“There was a boy,” she said, “and he was a king’s son, and he was the best of them. That’s not me talking. Everybody said it. He was straight and he was good and he was the only one in the whole family worth a damn.”
Somebody in the bleachers laughed at worth a damn and somebody else shushed them.

“And the king’s wife — she wasn’t his mother, his mother was gone — she took a shine to him. And when he wouldn’t have her, she went to the king and she said the boy had come after her. And she cried when she said it, and she was good at it, and the king believed her.”
She had them. She could feel it. It was the strangest sensation she had ever had, eight hundred people going quiet in a body.

“So they said, all right. There’s a way to settle this. And they built two fires.” Her voice did something on fires and she let it. “Two mountains of thorn wood, a hundred yards apart, and they lit them both, and they said: if you’re innocent, ride through. Ride between them. And if you’re telling the truth, God’ll bring you out the other side.”
“Did he do it?” a woman shouted.

“He did it,” Alma said. “He put on white. He got up on a black horse and he rode into the fire in white clothes in front of the whole country, and there was so much smoke nobody could see anything for a long time, and everybody stood there. And then he came out the other side.”
The bleachers made a sound.
“Not a mark on him,” she said. “Not a mark on the horse. Not a hair of it burned.”
She let it sit the way she had watched Doyle let things sit for four weeks.

“And it didn’t matter,” Alma said. “That’s the thing I come to tell you. He proved it in front of God and everybody and it did not matter one bit. His father couldn’t look at him after. Couldn’t stand him in the house. Sent him off to a war on the other side of the world to be rid of the shame of what he’d nearly done to him.” She was crying now and she did not stop. “And they killed him out there. They cut his throat over a basin and they poured him out on the ground like he was nothing, and he was twenty-some years old, and he had never done one wrong thing in his life.”
Somewhere in the second row a woman was crying with her.

“And I want to tell you what happened where the blood went in,” Alma said. “A plant come up. Out of the dirt. Right where it soaked in. It come up green and it kept coming up green and they couldn’t kill it and it’s growing there yet.”
She stopped.
The first coin came down before she had the microphone away from her mouth.
Twenty-two dollars and forty cents.
It took four men eleven minutes to sweep it and Ida counted it in a cigar box and Doyle stood over her while she did it and did not touch any of it, which Alma noticed.
“Twenty-two forty,” Ida said.

“That’s a record,” Doyle said. He sounded genuinely delighted. “That’s a record for this outfit and I’ve been running it since ’29.” He looked at Alma and there was nothing in his face but professional pleasure. “Where’d you get all that?”
“I made it up.”
“Sure you did,” Doyle said, and laughed, and went to find the band.
Bahram was on the far side of the floor when she came back out and he had not moved for the whole of it.
They walked half a circuit before either of them spoke.
“Siyavash,” he said.
“Yes.”
“You got the horse wrong. It was black, that is correct. You did not say his name.”
“I didn’t want to say his name.”
“No,” Bahram said. “I noticed that.”
They went around. The bleachers were emptying. Fitz was playing something slow.
“Say the thing,” Alma said.
“I am not going to say a thing.”
“Say it. You’ve been holding it for twenty minutes.”
He walked her past the bandstand.

“You told eight hundred people a story about a boy who was accused of something he did not do,” Bahram said, “and who proved it in front of everyone, and who was destroyed anyway. And they gave you twenty-two dollars.” He took the corner. “And I sat here and watched you and I could not work out whether you had chosen it or whether it had chosen you, and I have decided I do not want to know, and I am not going to ask, because I told you in the first week that I would not ask you anything.”
Alma said nothing at all.

“It is a beautiful story,” he said. “It is one of the two or three most beautiful things in the poem and I gave it to you nine days ago and now it is worth twenty-two dollars and forty cents.” He was looking straight ahead. “I am not angry with you. I want to be clear. I am trying to work out whether I am angry with myself for teaching you or with him for building the machine, and while I am working it out I would like to keep walking and not talk.”
So they kept walking and did not talk.
At the horn he said, without any preamble at all:
“Do it again next week.”
“What?”

“Do it again,” Bahram said. “Twenty-two dollars is twenty-two dollars, and you will be off this floor sooner than either of us wants, and I would rather you left here with something in your hand.” He held the door for her, and stood back, and said, “After you.”
And she was too tired to argue about the door, and went through first, and that was the only time in eleven hundred hours it happened.
17. SEVEN TRIALS
They built it over four nights in the last week of October and it was the only thing either of them ever made.

It started because of the foot. She could do the Jamshid turn thirty times an hour and it bought her three steps of relief each time, and by the six hundred and twentieth hour she was doing it so often that Doyle had begun calling it out from the microphone — there she goes, folks, there’s that spin — and the crowd had started to expect it.
“We need more of them,” Alma said.
“More turns?”
“More stories that don’t hurt.”
Bahram walked her four or five steps.
“There are seven,” he said.
He explained the shape of it first, at three in the morning, with the bleachers down to twenty people.

“There is a man called Rostam and he is the largest thing in the poem. Everything else in six hundred years bends around him. And early on, when he is young, the king of the country is taken prisoner in a place full of devils and blinded, and Rostam has to go and get him.”
“Alone?”
“With his horse.” He said it with a straight face. “The horse is a character. I want that understood.”
“The one he tested every horse in the country to find.”

“That one. Rakhsh.” He turned her. “And the road is seven days long and there is one thing on each day, and you have to get through all seven, and that is the whole of it. Seven. They are called the Seven Trials and every child where I am from can count them off on their fingers.”
“So teach me the seven.”

“I am not going to teach you the seven,” Bahram said. “I am going to build you the seven, and it is going to take four nights, and at the end of it you will have seven things you can do with your feet when your feet are finished. That is not a story. That is a tool.”
The first was the lion.

Rostam sleeps and the horse fights the lion alone and kills it and does not wake him, and in the morning Rostam is angry — if you had died, how would I have got there on foot? — which was, Bahram said, the single most Persian sentence in sixty thousand lines: a man being furious with a horse for saving his life inefficiently.
The step was a drop and a recovery. She let her weight go on the good foot for a half-beat and he took it and gave it back. It moved eleven pounds off the bad arch for the length of a bar.
The second was the desert with no water.

Three days of it. The horse going down. Rostam walking with his shield up against the sun and lying down to die, and then a ram walking past him, and he follows the ram because a ram must be going somewhere, and it goes to water.
The step was a long slow sideways trail, four counts, weight almost entirely on the left leg, the right foot only skimming the maple. It was the best of the seven. She could do it for a full chorus.
The third was the dragon.

It came out of the dark three times and twice the horse woke him and twice he saw nothing and shouted at the horse, and the third time he saw it. The step was a fast double turn, both feet on the balls, and it was the only one of the seven that hurt, and she kept it because it woke her up.
The fourth was the witch.
She came to him as a beautiful girl with a cup of wine and sat down beside him and he did not know what she was, and he said a blessing over the wine, and the moment he said it her face came off.
“That is the one,” Bahram said, “that people remember wrong. They think he saw through her. He did not see through her. He said a thing out of habit and it was the habit that saved him.”
The step was a stop. A dead stop on both feet, one count, and then away. It was the only thing in the whole four nights that was not motion and it was worth more than the rest of them together.
The fifth was the man in the reeds.
Rostam catches a watchman by the ears and the head comes off in his hand. There was no step for the fifth. Bahram tried three and threw them all out.
“Some of them are only a sentence,” he said. “Not everything has to be a step. Leave it.”
The sixth was the giant.

A thing the size of a hill that fights him with a tree in each hand, and Rostam beats it, and this was the only one Bahram would not simplify — he did the whole thing, all of it, in the two hours before dawn on the third night, and Alma held onto his shoulders and let herself be moved and did not have to think for a hundred and ten minutes.
The step was a lift. Not much of one — an inch, maybe two, on the second beat of every bar, both her feet coming off the maple entirely for a half-second while he took all of her.
“You can’t do that all night.”

“No,” Bahram said. “You may have it four times an hour and no more, and you are going to have to keep count yourself, because I will give it to you every time you ask and then in a week I will not be able to walk.”
The seventh was the White Div.

The devil in the cave, in the dark. Rostam goes in blind and they fight and it takes off his hand — no, she had that wrong, he took off its hand, and then its head — and there was blood, and the blood was the point, because you had to bring the blood back and put it in the king’s eyes and that was what gave the man his sight again.
“His blood cures blindness.”
“His blood cures blindness,” Bahram agreed. “Do not ask me why. It is a thousand years old. It has been asked.”

The step for the seventh was the biggest thing they made. Six counts, all the way around, a full circle with the man as the axis and her weight passed off her right foot three separate times inside it. It looked, from the bleachers, like the fanciest thing on the floor. It was pure engineering.
They ran the whole set for the first time on the thirty-first of October at about four in the morning and it took eleven minutes and nobody saw it.
There were nine people in the bleachers. Fitz was alone at the piano. Chick and Dot were on the far side, moving in a slow figure with their heads down on each other.

Alma went through all seven, in order, in the middle of an empty maple floor, and at the end of it she was upright and her foot was under her and she had not spoken a word for a quarter of an hour and had not needed to.
“That’s it,” she said. “That’s all seven.”
“That is all seven.”
“How long will it hold me?”
“I do not know.”
“Guess.”

“A week,” Bahram said. “Perhaps ten days. Then your left will come down and we will have to build the whole thing again backward, and there will not be time.” He was breathing hard. “Do not ask me the next question.”
“I wasn’t going to.”
“You were.”
She was. She let it go.

Doyle put it in the show inside of three days, and by the first week of November there was a thing at the Rialto that the Free Press called the Persian dance, and eleven hundred people came out on a Saturday night in the fourth year of the Depression to see a woman in a green dress do it.
Nobody in that building ever knew what any of it was.

They did not know that the drop was a lion, or that the long trail across the floor was three days without water, or that the dead stop on both feet was a man saved by a habit he had not thought about. They knew it was pretty. They knew the girl with the bad foot did seven things in a row and that the last one went all the way around.

Alma Sutter did the Seven Trials of Rostam eleven or twelve times a night for the last three weeks of that contest in front of a paying crowd in Ecorse, Michigan, and she did them again forty years later in a kitchen in Dearborn with nobody watching, holding the edge of a sink, at seventy-one years old, and she still had all seven.
18. NURSE’S ROUND
Ida changed the bottle for the third time on the second of November and this time she said so.
“It’s stronger.”
“How much stronger.”
“Hon,” Ida said, “there’s fourteen couples and he wants six by Sunday.” She poured out the tin cup. “You can say no.”
“Can I?”
“You can say no,” Ida said, “and Chick and Dot will say yes, and Sunday you’ll be on Beaufait Street.”
Alma drank it.
It came on in ninety seconds.

That was the first wrong thing. It had always taken twenty minutes and then four, and this went through her in the time it took to walk from the hatch to the door of the parts department, and by the time she was on the maple her jaw had locked.

Not clenched. Locked. She put her hand up to her own face and could not open it and stood in the middle of the floor with her fingers on her own chin at eleven o’clock at night, in front of six hundred people, trying to work out whether she was going to be able to speak again.
“Alma.”
She got it open. It made a sound.
“I’m all right.”
“You are not all right, your pupils are — ” Bahram took her chin and turned her face to the light and then let go as though it had burned him. “Do not take that again.”
“You had it too.”
“I am going to be sick in about an hour and I would like you not to look at me when it happens,” he said. “Take my hand. Do not take that again.”
Here is what she was able to say about the next nine hours, and she only ever said it once, in 1958, to a doctor who had asked her a different question.
The sound stopped being sound.

The cymbal was a hand on her face and she had known that for two weeks, but now the piano had edges, and the edges went into her arms, and a chord was not a noise, it was a shape that arrived at the skin and had corners on it. When Fitz went up the keyboard she felt it go up her spine, note by note, like somebody walking two fingers.
The light had a rim. Every light. The pendant lamp over the middle of the floor had a green ring around it about a foot wide and the ring was not still.

And the horn — she knew the horn was coming forty seconds before it came, every time, because the room got tight, and when it went off she was not able to keep her hands down. Twice she screamed. She knew she screamed because she saw the crowd react, and she could not hear herself do it, and after the second time Bahram put his hand flat over her sternum for a moment, which was not something he had ever done, and said, “You are in a building in Michigan and there are nine days left.”
At two in the morning the floor tilted and did not come back.

The whole maple went over about fifteen degrees toward the bandstand and stayed there, and she went with it, and there was no argument to be had with it — the floor was tilted, that was simply the state of the floor. She danced on a hill for four hours. She found that she was leaning against the slope with her whole body and that her right foot was uphill, which was a mercy, and she thought quite clearly: this is the best thing that has happened to my foot in three weeks.
At three she watched a man in the second row take his face off and put it in his lap.

He did it casually, the way you’d take off a hat. Then he put it back on. Then he did it again. Alma watched him do it maybe fifteen times and felt nothing at all about it, and it was only afterward, days later, that she understood the true horror of that hour was not the man. It was that she had watched it and had not been frightened, because being frightened would have required believing she was somewhere that things like that did not happen.
At half past three the bird came back.

She was ready for it this time. It was in the girders and it came all the way across the roof, gold and blue, flat as a window, and it settled with its wings out over the whole of the building. And Alma, going around the tilted floor with her head on a man’s shoulder, said out loud:
“You came.”
“What?”
“Not you.”
Bahram looked up at the roof.
“Is she here?”
“She’s here.”
He was quiet for a moment. Then he said, “Good,” and kept walking, and Alma loved him for it in a way she was not able to examine for another thirty-nine years.

He was sick at four, behind the bandstand, and she stood in front of him with her back turned so that no judge coming past would have a clear line, and afterward he wiped his mouth on his sleeve and said, “Thank you,” and they went back out.
At six the tilt came off the floor.
At seven Ida came down the row with the small bottle and Alma turned her face to the wall.
“It’s the down one, hon.”
“I don’t want it.”

“You want it,” Ida said. “You don’t take the down one after the up one, you’ll lay there for fifteen minutes with your eyes open and your heart going and you’ll come out worse than you went in.” She held out the cup. “That’s the whole racket. That’s how it works. Up one, down one, up one, down one, and that’s why nobody who does one of these ever quite comes right afterward.”
Alma took it.
“Ida,” she said. “How long have you known that?”
“Eleven years.”
“And you pour it anyway.”

Ida capped the bottle and put it in the tray with the others and stood there a moment with her hand on the cot rail, an old woman with a bricklayer’s hands at seven in the morning in a room that used to be where they kept the carburetors.
“There’s a bottle in that tray for me too,” she said. “You want to see it?”
Alma did not answer.
“Get your fifteen,” Ida said.
It was three days before her hands were right and she never again went a whole day without the rim on the lights.

That was the other thing she did not know at the time and worked out later, over years: it did not stop when the contest stopped. She had the rim on the lights in 1934. She had it in 1941, faintly, on winter afternoons. In 1971 she could still, if the room was dim enough and she was tired enough, look at a bare bulb and see the green ring standing an inch off it, not quite still, and she never told anybody about it, and she never entirely minded it either.
19. THE PAPERWORK
Doyle sent Ida for her at ten past two in the afternoon on the fourth of November.
“He wants you in the office.”
“I’ve got nine minutes.”
“He knows what you got,” Ida said, and would not look at her, and that was how Alma knew before she stood up.
The office had a window onto the floor with a blind half down. Doyle was behind the desk with the ledger shut and his hands flat on top of it and there was a second chair, which there had never been.
“Sit down.”
“I’ll stand.”
“Alma,” he said, “sit down. You got about eleven minutes and I don’t want to spend four of ’em on that.”
She sat down.

He did not do anything for a moment. He looked at his own hands on the ledger. Then he opened the top drawer and took out a manila envelope with a string closure and unwound the string and laid three sheets of paper on the desk and turned them around.
She did not need to read them.
She read them anyway, the way you touch a stove after you already know.
WAYNE COUNTY — SURRENDER OF CHILD FOR CARE — 11
JULY 1932. Her own signature at the bottom of the first page in a hand she did not recognize as hers, because her hand had been shaking. SUTTER, RUTH ANN. AGE 4 YR 2 MO. MOTHER:
SUTTER, ALMA. FATHER: SUTTER, ROY — WHEREABOUTS UNKNOWN.
And a second sheet, a carbon, stamped in October: STATUS —
RESIDENT.
“Sit back,” Doyle said. “You’ve gone grey.”
“When did you get these.”
“Fourteenth of October.”
“How.”

“I sent a fella.” He said it without any embarrassment at all. “I always send a fella. Every contest, every town — first two weeks I run down everybody that’s still standing. It’s not personal, sweetheart, it’s the business. I got twenty-two couples telling me twenty-two stories and I need to know which ones I can put on a handbill without some brother-in-law turning up with a lawyer.”
“You’ve had them three weeks.”
“I’ve had ’em three weeks.”
“And you never said.”
“No,” Doyle said. “I did not.”
Alma put her hands flat on her knees to stop them.
“Are you throwing me out?”
And Doyle Ferrin looked genuinely surprised, and then he laughed — not unkindly, he was never unkind, that was the thing she could never get past — and he said:
“Throwing you out?”

“Honey,” he said, and leaned forward, “I got a woman on my floor who’s been on her feet nine hundred and eighty hours on a busted arch and does that Persian thing that put eleven hundred people in here Saturday, and you think I want you out?”
“I lied on the form.”
“Everybody lies on the form.”
“It says — ” her voice went “ — it says that all statements given upon entry are true.”

“It says that so I can throw you out if I want to throw you out,” Doyle said. “That’s the whole reason it’s on there. That’s what a form is.” He sat back. “I ain’t throwing you out. I want to talk to you about the eighteenth.”
“The eighteenth of what?”

“November,” Doyle said. “That’s where this ends. That’s my last date, the hall’s let to a fella selling tractors after that, and I got to be in Fort Wayne on the twenty-second.” He tapped the desk twice. “Fourteen couples. Election’s Tuesday and my gate is going to fall through the goddamn floor, because there ain’t a soul in Wayne County going to pay a quarter to watch you walk while there’s returns coming in. Wednesday I’ll have two hundred people. Thursday I’ll have a hundred. And then I got to run this thing another ten days on a hundred people a night.”
“That’s not my — ”
“It’s about to be.” Doyle put one finger on the papers. “I want to bring her here.”
The room did something. She was aware of the blind, half down, and of the band starting up through the wall, and of a fly on the inside of the window.
“What?”
“I want to bring the little girl here,” Doyle said, “and put her in your arms in front of a full house.”
“No.”
“Hear it out.”
“No.”

“Alma.” He said her name the way he said things into the microphone, warm, unhurried, and it worked, it always worked. “Listen to what I’m actually saying. You went out there Saturday and you told ’em about a boy that rode through a fire and they threw twenty-two dollars on my floor. Twenty-two dollars for a story you made up.” He spread his hands. “This one’s true. This one’s a mother that put her baby in a county home in July because she couldn’t feed her, and danced six weeks to get her back. That ain’t a stunt. That’s the whole country. That is every single person in that bleacher and their sister.”
“You’d put her on a floor.”
“I’d put her in your arms.”
“For a quarter a head.”

“For a quarter a head,” Doyle agreed, “and you’d walk out of here with your daughter and eight or nine hundred dollars of silver, and I’d walk out with a full house on a Wednesday, and I don’t see the part where anybody’s hurt. That’s what I don’t see and I’ve been sitting on these three weeks looking for it.”
Alma stared at him.
“You’ve been sitting on it three weeks.”
“That’s right.”
“Why?”
“Because I needed a bad night to spend it on,” Doyle said simply. “There’s no point in it in October. It’s worth nothing on a Saturday when I’m full anyway.”
“He doesn’t know,” she said.
“Who? The Sheik?” Doyle shook his head. “No. And I ain’t going to tell him. That’s yours to tell or not tell, I don’t get in the middle of that.”
“You put me with him.”
“I did.”
“Why me?” Alma said. “Off the card. Number sixty-three. Out of ninety-one couples you had a man on the payroll and you gave him me — why?”
Doyle looked at her for a moment.

“Because you come in alone,” he said, “and you told me at that table that you had a little girl and that you had her in July, and you didn’t cry when you said it.” He shrugged, and it was the most honest thing she ever saw him do. “Sweetheart, a woman that don’t cry when she says that is a woman that’s got a long way left in her. I knew you’d go three weeks before you took your coat off.”
The horn went through the wall.
Alma stood up. Her legs held, which surprised her.
“How long do I have to answer.”
“Sunday.”
“And if I say no?”

“Then you say no,” Doyle said, “and we go on as we are, and you dance till the eighteenth and you take whatever you take, and I’ll shake your hand at the door and mean it.” He was already reaching for the ledger. “And you’ll be about two hundred short of the year at the county home, and they charge by the quarter, and they’ll have had her four months by Christmas.”
He said that last part while he was opening the book. Not as a threat. As a fact he happened to know, offered in passing, because he had sent a fella and the fella had been thorough.
Alma went out onto the floor and put her hand in Bahram’s and did not say one word about any of it for four days.
20. ECORSE ROAD
He asked Doyle for four hours on the Saturday morning and Doyle gave them to him.
Alma found out about it at eleven o’clock, on the floor, from a judge.
“Sixty-three, you’re soloing this afternoon.”
“I’m what?”
“Your partner’s got leave. Twelve to four. You’ll solo or you’ll take a spare and there ain’t a spare, so you’ll solo.” The judge was already walking off. “Same rules. Knees don’t touch.”
She got hold of him at the twelve o’clock horn, in the corridor, with one hand in his shirt.
“Where are you going.”
“Out.”
“Where.”
“I will be back at four.”
“Where, Bahram.”
He looked at her, and she watched him decide not to lie, and she watched him decide not to answer either, which was worse.
“I am going to be gone four hours,” he said, “and you are going to walk for four hours by yourself, and I am sorry about it, and it is the only thing I have asked this building for in six weeks.”
“You’re on his payroll — ”

“Yes. That is why he said yes.” Bahram took her hand off his shirt, not roughly, and held it a moment. “Alma. Do the seven. Do them in order and start again at the top and do not count the hours. Four hours is eleven rounds.”
“Tell me where you’re going.”
“No,” he said, and went.
Four hours alone on a maple floor.

She had not been alone on it since the twenty-fourth of September. Not for one minute of one hour, waking or otherwise, and she had not understood until that Saturday afternoon that the whole apparatus of her survival was a man’s body, and that without it she was a woman of twenty-nine with a collapsed arch walking in a circle in a room.
There was nothing to lean on. That was the first thing. She kept reaching.

There was nobody to talk. That was the second, and it was worse, and by the second hour she was talking out loud to herself in a low voice, saying the seven off on her fingers — lion, desert, dragon, witch, reeds, giant, div — and a judge came over at one point and put two fingers under her chin to check her eyes, and she said “I’m fine,” and he said, “I know. You’re saying things.”

The bleachers had maybe a hundred and fifty people in them. It was a matinée in the fourth year of the Depression and there was a woman in a green dress walking alone in the middle of an empty floor doing seven strange figures over and over, and after about ninety minutes of it, Alma realised that they had gone quiet.
Not gone away. Quiet. A hundred and fifty people in a dim room watching a woman by herself, and nobody eating, and nobody talking.
Chick came past on the outside in the third hour with Dot asleep on his shoulder.
“You’re all right,” he said.
“I’m not all right.”
“You’re upright.” He steered Dot around the corner. “That’s the whole of it, kid. Everything else is decoration.”
Bahram came back at four minutes past four.

She saw him come in the fire door at the far end and cross the floor toward her, and she was already going toward him, and he took her hands and put her straight back into the circle without breaking stride.
“You’re back.”
“Yes.”
“Where were you.”
“Alma — ”
“Where were you.”
He walked her a full half circuit before he said anything, and when he did he said:
“Do you remember that I told you I would not ask you anything?”
She stopped breathing.

“I have kept that,” Bahram said. “For six weeks. I have never once asked you a question about July and I am not going to start today and I am not going to answer one either. That is the same promise. It only looks different from this side.”
“That’s not — that’s not the same thing at all — ”
“It is exactly the same thing,” he said, “and I need you to let it be, and I am asking you, and I have never asked you for anything.”
Here is what she noticed over the next thirty hours, and she noticed all of it and made nothing of any of it until Wednesday.

His coat. He had gone out in the brown coat he had come in with and he came back with it buttoned in a room that was seventy degrees and he did not take it off for the rest of the contest, not once, not on the floor, not at cot call, and when Ida told him to take it off he said no.
He stopped taking the Cordial. Ida came down the row and he shook his head, and she said, “You’ll go out,” and he said, “Yes,” and did not take it, and did not take it the next time either.
He walked on her right and would not swap.

And he stopped telling her anything new. That was the one she should have seen, because it was the only thing in six weeks he had ever been reliable about. For thirty hours he did not start a single story. He talked — he talked constantly, he talked about the band and the mop and the price of coffee in Constantinople in 1923 — and there was not one king in any of it.
She asked him, on the Sunday morning, why he’d stopped.
“I have not stopped.”
“You’ve stopped.”
Bahram walked her past the bandstand.
“There is one left,” he said.
“One?”

“There is one story left that matters and it is the largest one and I have been keeping it since the first week.” He was looking straight ahead. “I had thought I would give it to you at the end. I have changed my mind. I am going to give it to you tonight and tomorrow, because I do not think it should be the last thing.”
“Why not?”
“Because it takes two days to tell,” Bahram said, “and I do not know how many I have.”
That afternoon she went into the office and told Doyle Ferrin yes.

It took under a minute. Doyle did not gloat and did not smile and did not shake her hand. He wrote three words in the ledger and said, “Wednesday. Four o’clock, that’s hour eleven hundred, I’ll put it on the bills tomorrow,” and then he said something she thought about a great deal afterward.
“You want my advice?”
“No.”
“Tell the Sheik.”
Alma stood in the doorway.
“Why.”

“Because I’ve run ninety of these,” Doyle said, “and the thing that busts a couple at the end ain’t the feet.” He shut the ledger. “It’s one of ’em carrying something the other one don’t know about. Every time. Ninety contests.”
“You’d know.”
“I would know,” Doyle agreed, entirely without irony, and reached for the telephone.
21. WHAT HE DIDN’T SAY
“There was a man,” Bahram said, “and he was the strongest man who ever lived, and he was the one I told you about at the horses.”
“Rostam.”

“Rostam.” He took her hands and squared her up the way he did when it was going to be a long one. “And one day he went hunting on the border, alone, and he ate too much and he fell asleep under a tree, and while he was asleep some men stole his horse.”
“The horse he spent years finding.”

“The horse he spent years finding. Yes. Good.” He turned her. “So he walked. He was too proud to go home without it, so he walked into the country on the other side of the border — the enemy country, the one they had been fighting for two hundred years — and he came to a city, and he went in and said who he was.”
“And they didn’t kill him?”

“They gave him a feast,” Bahram said. “That is the part you have to understand about this poem or nothing in it makes sense. The king of the enemy country knew exactly who he was and put him at the head of the table and gave him wine, because you do not kill a guest, not even that guest, and because Rostam was famous everywhere and being able to say he had eaten in your house was worth more than his life.”
“And that night the king’s daughter came to his room.”
“Oh,” Alma said.

“Her name was Tahmineh. And she came in and stood there and told him the truth, which is that she had heard about him her entire life, that men had been telling stories about him in her father’s hall since she was small, and that she had decided as a girl that if she ever had a child it would be his.” He steered them past the stage. “She did not flirt. She did not pretend to be lost in the corridor. She came in and said: I want a child from you and then you may go.”
“And he — ”

“He said yes,” Bahram said. “He sent for a priest that night and they were married before morning, because he was not a man who would do it otherwise. I want that in the record too. They were married.”
“How long did he stay?”
Bahram walked her three steps.
“One night,” he said.

“In the morning he took off his arm-band — a thing he wore, a clasp, and it was known, everybody in the world knew that band — and he gave it to her and he said: if it is a girl, put this in her hair. If it is a boy, put it on his arm.”
“And then he left.”

“They found his horse the next day and he left.” Bahram’s voice had not changed at all. “And he went home, and he did not send for her, and he did not go back, and in nine months she had a son and she called him Sohrab, and she put the band on his arm.”
The band was four men. Fitz was playing something with a lot of air in it.
“Did she write to him?”
“She wrote to him.”
“Did he write back?”

“He sent money,” Bahram said, “and gifts, and he sent word that he was pleased. He was not a monster. He was a man with a country to defend on the other side of a war and a child in the enemy’s house and he did what men do, which is that he meant to go, every year, and then it was another year.”
Alma had her head down on his shoulder.
“So the boy grew up without him,” she said.

“The boy grew up enormous.” And there was, for one moment, something that was almost joy in his voice. “That is the thing about Sohrab. He is his father’s son in every particular. At ten he could beat any man in the city. At twelve nobody would fight him. He was the biggest thing anyone there had ever seen and he had never once been told who his father was, because his mother was frightened.”
“Frightened of what?”
“That Rostam would send for him. That she would lose him.” He turned her under his arm. “And that her own father would kill the boy if he found out whose he was. Both. Every day, both.”
“Did he ask?”

“He asked constantly,” Bahram said. “He asked from the time he could speak. Who am I. Why am I bigger than everybody. Where is my father. And she told him nothing for fourteen years, and then one day he came and stood in front of her and would not leave, and she told him.”
“And what did he do?”
Bahram walked her a long way before he answered, right around the outside of the floor, past the bleachers and the fire door and the bandstand and the fourteen other couples moving in the dark.
“He raised an army,” he said.
“To fight him?”

“To find him.” He said it with a force she had not heard from him in six weeks. “That is the whole tragedy and it is right there in the middle of it and everybody misses it. He did not go to fight his father. He went to war against his father’s country in order to locate his father. Because he was seventeen and enormous and he had been told a name, and the only thing he could think of that would bring a man like that out of a place like that was an invasion.”
“That’s insane.”
“He was seventeen,” Bahram said. “You are trying to solve the largest problem of your life with the only tool you have. And the only tool he had was that he was the strongest boy on earth.”
Alma lifted her head off his shoulder.
“And the plan was — ”

“The plan was very simple and it very nearly worked. He would break the border. Rostam would be sent for, because Rostam was always sent for. They would meet. And he would say: I am your son. And then, he thought — this is in the poem, he says it out loud to his mother before he goes — then the two of them together would be so strong that they could put whoever they liked on both thrones and there would never be a war again.”
“Oh God.”
“Yes.”
“Barney — ”
“That is where I am stopping,” Bahram said.
“You can’t stop there.”
“I am stopping there.”
“Barney.”
“Tomorrow.” He was walking her toward the gap in the bleachers because the horn was forty seconds out; she could feel it coming through the floor. “I told you it takes two days.”
“Just tell me — ” she had hold of his shirt again “ — just tell me whether the boy finds him.”
Bahram stopped at the gap.

He looked down at her for what was probably two seconds and was certainly not longer, and there was something on his face that she had never seen there before and did not see again until Wednesday afternoon.
“He finds him,” he said.
The horn went off.
22. SOHRAB
He told it on the Monday night and he told it badly.

That was the thing she came back to. Six weeks of a man who put a sentence down like a full cup, and on the seventh of November 1932, from about eleven at night until nearly four in the morning, he told her the largest story he had and he could not do it. He stopped in the middle of it. He went back and did pieces again. Twice he lost the thread entirely and stood there with his mouth working and she had to say the tent, you were at the tent, and he said, “Yes. The tent.”
She thought it was the Cordial coming out of him. He had not taken it in three days.

“They met on the field,” he said. “There is a fortress on the border and the boy took it in an afternoon, and the king sent for Rostam, and Rostam came — late, drunk, four days late, because he had been sent for a hundred times and it had never once mattered.”
“Did he know who he was fighting?”
“Nobody knew. The boy was seventeen and no one had heard of him. He was simply the largest man anybody had seen since Rostam.”
“Did the boy know?”

“The boy suspected the whole time,” Bahram said. “That is the first thing. Sohrab looks across at this man and something goes through him and he asks. He asks him directly, in front of both armies. He says: I think you are Rostam.”
Alma had stopped walking properly and he corrected her with his knee.
“And?”
“And Rostam said no.”
“He lied?”

“He said, I am not Rostam. I am a servant of Rostam’s.” Bahram’s voice had gone flat. “And there is a reason for it and it is a good reason and it is the worst thing in the poem. He is old. He is the most famous man alive. And a boy he has never heard of has just taken a fortress in an afternoon, and Rostam looks at him and thinks: if this is the one who finally beats me, then let it be a nobody who beats a nobody. Let there not be a song about the day Rostam went down.”
“He lied about his own name to save his reputation.”
“He lied about his own name,” Bahram said, “because he could not bear to be seen losing. Yes. And every single thing that comes after is that one sentence.”
“They fought three times.”
“Three?”

“Three days.” He turned her at the corner. “The first day they broke every weapon they had. Spears, swords, clubs, all of it, and the horses gave out and neither of them could stand and they agreed to stop and come back in the morning. And that night the boy went back to his own tent and said to his people — I am quoting it — he said: he is like me. When I look at him something turns over in me. I think this is my father.”
“And they told him no.”

“They told him no.” Bahram was quiet for a moment. “A man in his own camp who knew the truth and had been sent along by the king specifically to prevent this, and he said: no, boy, I have seen Rostam and that is not him. And Sohrab believed him. Because he was seventeen and he wanted to be told what to do.”
“On the second day — ”
“On the second day the boy won.”
Alma looked up.

“He threw him,” Bahram said. “The strongest man who ever lived, on his back in the dirt in front of two armies, and Sohrab had a knife out and was on his chest. Seventeen years old. And Rostam said — ” he stopped. “He said: it is not our custom. It is our custom to let a man up the first time and take his head the second. And it is not true, there is no such custom, he made it up on the ground with a knife over him.”
“And the boy let him up.”
“The boy let him up.”
They went around the corner by the fire door. There were four people in the bleachers.
“Why?”

“Because he was decent,” Bahram said. “Because he was seventeen and decent and he wanted to be the kind of man his father would have been proud of, and he had no idea he was doing it in front of him.”
“The third day.”
“The third day he killed him.”
Bahram said it and kept walking and Alma had to make herself keep her feet going.
“They wrestled from morning. And Rostam got him — got a grip, got him over, and had the knife in him before the boy hit the ground, and it was fast, and it was over.”
“And then — ”

“And then the boy said a thing while he was dying.” He walked four steps. “He said: this is my own fault and nobody else’s. I came here to find my father and I have been asking for him all my life and now I am dying in a strange country and I never saw his face. And then he said: do not think you are safe. My father will hear of this. Whatever hole you go into, he will find you.”
“Oh God.”
“And Rostam laughed,” Bahram said. “He laughed. And he asked him, to be kind to a dying boy, he asked: who is your father, then? Tell me his name.
“And the boy said the name.
“And Rostam went down on the ground.”
The band had stopped. Fitz had gone. There was a phonograph playing at the back of the hall on a low table, some old thing, and it was hissing more than it was playing.

“He tore the shirt off him,” Bahram said, “looking for the arm-band. And it was there. On his arm. Exactly where his mother had put it seventeen years before, exactly where he had told her to put it, the day he left.”
Alma was crying. She had not decided to.

“He tried everything,” Bahram said. “There is a medicine — there is a thing the king has, and it heals anything, and Rostam sent a man to the king begging for it, and the king would not send it. Because if the boy lived, the two of them together would be stronger than any throne on earth, and the king knew it.” He turned her under his arm, slowly, the Jamshid turn, the one that cost her nothing. “And Rostam sat there holding him and the boy died before the man got back, and he would have died anyway, because the king was never going to send it.”
“That’s the end?”
“That is the end. He burned his own tents and he cut his horse’s tail and he went home and he lived another two hundred years and there is not one line in the rest of it about him being happy.”
They walked in silence for a long time.
“Why did you keep that one for last?” Alma said.
Bahram did not answer.
“Barney.”
“Because it is the best one,” he said.
“That’s not why.”
“No.”
She waited. She waited a full circuit of the floor, and past the bandstand, and around again.
“Ask me the question you want to ask,” he said at last, “and I will answer it, and it is the only one you will get.”

Alma thought about it for a long time. She had it. She had it right there — who are you in that story — and she stood on a collapsed arch at four in the morning on the eighth of November 1932 with a man’s arms around her and she was so tired that her mind put its hand on the wrong thing.
“Did Rostam ever tell anybody?” she said. “Afterward. Did he ever tell them what he’d done?”
Bahram walked her all the way around.
“No,” he said. “He said the boy was a stranger.”

And Alma said, “That’s the saddest thing I ever heard,” and put her head down on his shoulder, and went out for about ninety seconds, and came back up in a different corner of the room with his voice still going and no memory at all of what he had been saying while she was under.
23. TWO BITS AT THE DOOR
The handbills came off a press in River Rouge on the Monday afternoon and by Tuesday morning they were in every window in three towns.
WEDNESDAY 4 P.M. — HOUR 1100
SHE BURIED HER BABY IN JULY
AND SHE WANTS HER BACK
SEE IT HAPPEN ON THE FLOOR
25¢ — DOYLE FERRIN PRESENTS
Ida brought one in and put it on the cot without a word and went out again.
Alma read it four times.

Buried. He had left it in. She had told him the truth in that office with the blind half down, she had sat in a chair while he laid her own signature on the desk in front of her, and he had gone out and printed buried on eight hundred handbills, and it took her a full minute to work out why.
Because surrendered did not sell.

Because a woman whose child died was a woman the crowd could weep for, and a woman who had signed her daughter over to the county in July because she could not feed her was a woman the crowd would have to decide about, and Doyle Ferrin had never in ninety contests given a crowd anything to decide.
“Take it back.”
“Can’t. They’re up.”
“Then print another one.”

“Sweetheart.” Doyle had his coat on; he was going somewhere. “I got two hundred bills in windows from here to Wyandotte and a man in Toledo owed money and it’s Tuesday. What do you want me to do, go around with a bucket of paste?”
“It says buried.”
“It says something people’ll pay for.”
“It’s a lie.”

Doyle stopped in the doorway and turned around and for the first time in six weeks he looked at her with something other than professional warmth, and what was underneath it was not cruelty either, and that was the part she could never afterward explain to anybody.
It was patience.
“Alma,” he said, “you told me that at the table. On the twenty-fourth of September.” He put his hat on. “I wrote down what you said. All I ever did was print it.”
She did not tell Bahram.
She had four separate opportunities in the day that followed and she took none of them and she knew exactly what she was doing every time.

He would have seen a bill. That was the thing she kept in front of herself, the way you keep a hand in front of a candle. Everybody had seen one. They were in the window of the diner on the corner and in the drugstore and pasted to the fire door of the Rialto itself. He had been out of the building on Saturday and the bills went up on Monday, but there were fourteen couples in that hall and every one of them had one, and Chick had brought three back from a cigar store and left them around like a man leaving bait.
So he knew. He must know. And he had not said one word about it in twenty hours, and she told herself that meant he was letting her keep it, the way he had let her keep everything else.
That was the arithmetic she did on the eighth of November 1932 and it was the worst arithmetic she ever did in her life.
The verse went up on the Tuesday.

Doyle wrote it on the corner of the bandstand in pencil the way he wrote all of them and handed it down to Fitz, and Fitz looked at it for a second and then looked up at Doyle, and Doyle said, “Play it,” and Fitz played it.
The Persian prince and the girl in black,
She buried her baby and she wants her back,
Two bits at the door — come see her get it back.
So hold me up till the horn.
There were three hundred people in the hall and about a third of them already knew the tune, because the tune was six weeks old and had been in every kitchen in Ecorse since the middle of October.
By the second time through, they were singing it.

Alma Sutter danced in a circle on a maple floor with a man’s arms around her while three hundred people sang a song about her dead daughter, who was not dead, and she looked at the floor going by under her feet and thought, with a clarity she never had again about anything:
I did this. Nobody did this to me. I signed the paper in July and I lied at the table in September and I said yes on Sunday, and everything since has just been machinery.
She got through it. She did the seven. Lion, desert, dragon, witch, reeds, giant, div, and back to the top.
Bahram did not say anything about the verse.

He did something else. On the fourth time through, when the whole hall had it and the drummer had come in behind it, he stopped them dead in the middle of the floor — both feet, one count, the witch, the only still thing in the seven — and he put his hand flat on the back of her head and held it there against his shoulder so that she was facing into his shirt and not into the room.
He held it there for the whole verse. Eleven seconds, maybe twelve.
A judge started over and thought better of it.
And when the band went into the next thing he took his hand away and put it back on her waist and walked her on and said, in an ordinary voice, as though continuing a conversation about nothing:

“There were nine hundred people here on Saturday and there will be twelve hundred tomorrow and none of them will be able to tell you one true thing about either of us. That is not a small thing to have. Most people do not get it. Keep hold of it.”
Alma said, “Barney — ”
“I know,” he said.
She had not said anything yet.
“I know,” he said again. “It is all right.”
And she believed, for the next nineteen hours, that he was telling her he had seen the handbill and forgiven her for it.
IV. THE GRIND
24. THE ARGONNE FOREST
The last event Doyle Ferrin ever ran at the Rialto was called the Argonne Forest and it went on from midnight until twenty past three in the morning on the ninth of November 1932.

He had been saving it. It was a Sunday event in the program he ran in other towns and he had never used it in Ecorse because he had never needed it, and on election night, with the hall down to a hundred and ten people and a radio going behind the bandstand, he needed it.
The rules were that the men carried the women.

That was all. That was the whole event. The seven men picked up the seven women and carried them, and they kept walking, and every twenty minutes a judge blew a whistle and any man who had put his partner down since the last whistle was out.
It was named for the battle because Doyle had a poster.
The radio came on at eight and by ten it was over and everybody in the building knew it.

Alma heard the numbers the way you hear weather. Pennsylvania. Ohio. Michigan, which went, and the hundred and ten people in that hall made a sound at Michigan that was not quite a cheer — it was lower than a cheer, it went on longer — and a man near the fire door put both hands over his face and sat down.
Roosevelt had it by midnight. He had forty-two states before it was finished.

And Alma Sutter, twenty-nine years old, of Harlan County, Kentucky, and Beaufait Street, Detroit, who had not read a newspaper since the twenty-fourth of September and had no address to be registered at and had not voted, was in the middle of a maple floor being carried by a Persian who could not vote at all.
“Are you glad?” she said. It was the first thing she’d said in an hour.
Bahram shifted her weight.
“I do not know what it means,” he said. “I have been here eight years. In 1928 they said everything would change and it changed into this.”
“But are you glad.”
He walked eleven or twelve steps.

“There is a thing at the end of the poem,” he said. “After everything. After six hundred years of kings. The Arabs come over the border and it is finished, all of it, the whole world of the book, and the poet writes a letter from a general on the losing side to his brother, and the general says: I see what is coming and there is nothing to be done, and men who have nothing will be raised up, and men who have everything will be brought down, and the world will be turned over.” He shifted her again. “And it is not a hopeful letter and it is not a despairing one. It is a man saying: it is going to be different and I will not be able to tell you whether it was better, because I will be dead.”
“That’s not an answer.”

“No,” Bahram agreed. “I am glad. I am glad because a hundred and ten people in this room made that noise when they said Michigan, and I have not heard anybody in this country make that noise in four years.”
At eleven o’clock, before the Argonne started, Doyle Ferrin stood on the edge of the maple with the microphone and said, “Folks, I got a new one,” and handed a cigarette paper down to Fitz.

It was not a verse. It was the bridge — the part in the middle of a song where the tune goes somewhere else and then comes home — and it was the only bridge that song ever had, and he had been sitting on it since Sandusky.
Fitz played it slow, and the hundred and ten people who had stayed in that hall on election night instead of going home to a radio learned it in one pass:
Oh, they never say stop and they never say when,
They just count the hours and they count them again,
And the only three words in the American tongue
Are hold me up —
Hold me up till the horn.
Three couples went out in the Argonne Forest.
A man from Melvindale went down at half past one with his partner still in his arms and did not let go of her when he hit the maple, and Doyle gave them a beautiful send-off.

Chick Mullaly carried Dot for three hours and twenty minutes without setting her down once, and at the end of it he was walking like a man in water, and Dot was asleep with her face in his neck, and Alma watched them go by and thought about a boarding house that was never going to exist.
Bahram carried her for the whole of it.

He was thirty years old and he had lost twenty-two pounds since September and he had not taken the Cordial in five days, and he carried a woman for three hours and twenty minutes on the ninth of November 1932 and did not put her down.
She said, once, around two in the morning: “Put me down.”
“No.”
“Barney, they’ll — they’ll let you set me down and pick me up, that’s not the rule, the rule is — ”
“I know the rule.”
“Then put me down.”
“I am not going to put you down,” Bahram said, “because I am not going to be able to pick you up again, and I would rather not find that out tonight in front of these people.”
At twenty past three Doyle called it and there were seven couples left.
Seven. Nine days short of the eighteenth. Doyle stood on the bandstand under one work lamp and looked out at a hall with about sixty people in it and did the arithmetic in public.

“All right,” he said. “Here’s where we are. Hour eleven hundred is this afternoon at four o’clock, and that’s the finish. I can’t run this into next week and I’m not going to stand here and pretend otherwise.”
Somebody said, “The finish?”
